articles.title: Noah's Ark site yields first look at charred wood fragments recovered deep below soil
articles.summary: Sharing their findings with Fox News Digital, the Noah's Ark Research Project has recovered wood deep beneath the Durupinar Formation, but critical lab results are pending.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Researchers investigating a site in Turkey long believed by some to be the resting place of Noah's Ark have recovered what they describe as charred wood fragments from deep beneath the surface — and they shared exclusive photos and video of the findings with Fox News Digital. The Noah's Ark Research Project, which involves researchers affiliated with Turkish universities, has spent the last year collecting soil samples at the Durupınar site near Mount Ararat in eastern Turkey. Durupınar, a boat-shaped formation identified in 1959, has drawn speculation for many years over a possible connection to Noah's Ark — an assertion that geologists have resisted. SITE WHERE JESUS WAS CRUCIFIED AND BURIED REVEALS NEW EVIDENCE THAT BACKS BIBLICAL ACCOUNT In a 1996 paper, geologists Lorence Gene Collins and David Franklin Fasold disputed claims that the Durupinar Formation was Noah's Ark, arguing instead that it was "a natural rock structure." But the findings haven't deterred researchers from continuing to investigate the site. A university-backed project is now using deep-core drilling, ground-penetrating radar and laboratory analysis to examine the formation, including newly recovered wood fragments. The investigation has also involved radar surveys conducted by scientist Khosrow Bakhtar. The project says the scientist has reported identifying organized patterns and possible chambers and corridors beneath the roughly 515-foot-long formation. AUTHOR DINESH D'SOUZA CHALLENGES BIBLE SKEPTICS WITH 'STARTLING' ARCHAEOLOGICAL DISCOVERIES Researchers, meanwhile, have sent the recovered wood fragments for carbon-14 dating and species identification, while lab analysis of hundreds of soil and core samples remains underway. The fragments have not been independently linked to Noah's Ark, and laboratory testing has yet to establish their age or origins. Exclusive photos shared with Fox News Digital show several darkened, cracked fragments that researchers identify as charred wood, some of which appear to have visible grain patterns and growth rings. Speaking to Fox News Digital from Turkey, archaeologist Cenker Atila, who is overseeing the investigation, said the team recovered the fragments some 30 feet beneath the surface of the Durupınar formation. HOLY LAND DISCOVERY REVEALS ANCIENT CHARRED RELICS FROM ONE OF JERUSALEM'S DARKEST CHAPTERS Though the laboratory results on the wood's age are not yet available, Atila said that, in his professional opinion, the fragments "are very ancient." Atila, a professor of archaeology at Sivas Cumhuriyet University in Turkey, pointed to several features of the formation that he believes support the possibility of a connection to Noah's Ark. "Too many coincidences have come together to be ignored," he said. "The ship-shaped formation was found in the location described in the holy books. Its dimensions are consistent with those mentioned in the holy books, and its shape resembles a ship." Atila added, "The holy books describe Noah's Ark as having three levels, and the Durupinar formation also appears to have a three-level structure." ARCHAEOLOGISTS MAKE UNUSUAL FIND NEAR SITE WHERE ARK OF THE COVENANT WAS ONCE KEPT Atila said carbon content inside the formation is higher than outside it, another observation he believes supports the team's theory. "After presenting all this evidence, I leave it to those who read these reports to decide what they believe," he said. But Atila acknowledged that many unanswered questions remain. "Are the corridor-like and room-like structures actually parts of a ship? Do the wood fragments really belong to the ship? Will we find any traces of human or animal remains in the soil analyses? These are all very exciting questions, and I am eagerly awaiting the results," he said. LOST CITY TIED TO BIBLICAL EXODUS MAY HAVE FINALLY BEEN DISCOVERED IN EGYPT The researchers believe the wood discovery could mark a breakthrough in their efforts to determine whether the Durupınar formation is the remains of Noah's Ark. Lauren Witzke, director of marketing and fundraising for Noah's Ark Scans, told Fox News Digital that she believes the discovery proves "that this is not just a geological structure," challenging the long-held argument that the formation is natural. Witzke said that the project marks the first time research at the Durupınar formation has been conducted with official Turkish oversight, documented chain-of-custody procedures and independent laboratory testing. Witzke said she believes the discovery could have far-reaching religious and historical implications if ultimately linked to the biblical vessel. ANCIENT RITUAL COMPLEX UNEARTHED AT SITE TIED TO BIBLICAL CITY IN EZEKIEL: ‘STILL HOLDS MANY SECRETS’ "We won't know until we start getting results back from the labs," she said. "However, with that being said, it is world shaking. It's a world-shaking discovery." "As soon as it's confirmed by experts, we [will] share it with the world." Looking ahead, Witzke said the wood samples have been sent to four laboratories in four different countries for testing, with the team hoping to pursue further excavation in 2027. Once the results from the wood, soil and core samples are available, Atila plans to apply for additional excavation permits, she said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "We do believe that we have a very good chance to continue the research and excavate next year," Witzke said. The team also hopes its ongoing research will help address skepticism surrounding the site's possible connection to Noah's Ark. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Witzke said the project is crowdfunded and that researchers plan to share laboratory results and other findings with the public through their website, NoahsArkScans.com, as the investigation progresses. "We've been under a lot of scrutiny because we've been releasing the evidence as we go," she said. "As soon as it's confirmed by experts, we [will] share it with the world." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ In a previous interview with Fox News Digital, Andrew Jones, lead researcher with Noah's Ark Scans, acknowledged the team still had "a lot of work to do" before drawing conclusions about the site. As a Christian, Jones said he believes in the biblical account but understands why some remain skeptical of the project. "I can understand because I have friends who are atheists or agnostic, and they think that I’m looking for Santa’s house or something," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We still have the lab work to do," added Jones. "And I hope everyone can follow along and see what we find."

articles.title: Tories pledge to cut benefits for children with 'milder cases' of ADHD
articles.summary: Conservative shadow minister Helen Whately says the system risks putting children on a "conveyor belt" towards a "lifetime on benefits".
articles.body:
The Conservatives have pledged to save £2.8bn a year by ending Disability Living Allowance (DLA) payments to families of children with "milder cases" of behavioural disorders, learning difficulties or ADHD.

The policy is one of a series of measures which the party says will save £36bn from the welfare budget.

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said the system risked putting children on a "conveyor belt" towards a "lifetime on benefits".

Labour described the Tories' plan as a "charter for homelessness and human misery that would push people into hardship and end up costing the state more".

DLA for children allows parents to claim between £30.30 and £194.60 per week to help cover the additional costs that come with raising a disabled child.

The child must either have difficulty getting about or need more looking after than a child of the same age who does not have a disability.

The Conservatives say child DLA is the "fastest growing benefit in the UK's welfare system", citing government statistics showing the number of cases had risen from 521,476 in 2020 to 914,000.

The party is proposing that in cases where a claim is for a behavioural disorder, learning difficulty or ADHD, only those with the highest need will be eligible for cash payments.

Under the party's plans, those with the most severe conditions, representing around 30% of cases, would continue to receive payments.

The remaining 70% would lose the money but instead receive support through mental health services and family hubs, into which the Conservatives have said they will invest £1bn.

The changes would apply to new claims and reassessments. Those with physical disabilities would be exempt.

The party's other previously-announced cuts include:

£13.7bn from changes to sickness and disability benefits including restricting payments to claimants with "milder mental health issues and neurodiversity conditions such as anxiety, depression and ADHD"

£9.5bn by making it harder for foreign nationals to claim benefits

£4.5bn by reducing local housing allowance payments

£3.1bn by reintroducing the two-child benefit cap

Setting out the party's plans, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "The reality is that millions of people can and do contribute to our economy, to their families, to their communities even when they face serious challenges.

"Double amputees run marathons. People who are housebound do wonderful creative work from home. People with autism run some of the biggest tech companies in the world.

"If you tell a young person that their ADHD means they are defective and will never amount to anything, that mindset is likely to be more destructive to their future than the condition itself."

What are the government's options for reducing welfare spending?

How a rise in ADHD benefits claims is adding to welfare spending challenge

'Worrying' number of teens lose disability benefits

The Labour government has said it wants to bring the benefits bill down but has not set out a timetable for any reductions.

More details of its plans are expected to come after former minister Alan Milburn has published his review on young people not in education, employment and training.

Both Milburn's review and a review into disability benefits, co-chaired by Minister Sir Stephen Timms, will be published in November.

Asked about Milburn's review, Whately said he was "rolling the pitch for more welfare spending" adding: "We're in no question and no doubt that you can make savings from welfare - it's just that Labour doesn't want to do that."

A Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives designed and implemented this benefit system, which has driven large numbers of people to be signed off and written off.

"Labour is tackling the collapse in face-to-face assessments, bringing in personalised employment support for sick and disabled people and spreading opportunity to young people through the Youth Guarantee."

The Child Poverty Action Group said: "These proposals would take the UK back to the dark ages, causing the biggest overnight increase in child poverty since records began."

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said: "Until the Conservatives face up to the damage their botched Brexit deal has done, they will remain an out-of-touch, anti-growth, anti-business party, and it will be disabled people and children growing up in poverty who will pay the price."

articles.title: Nvidia's AI chips: The technology China wants and America won't share
articles.summary: America wants to keep its most powerful AI chips out of China's hands. But China is also a market Nvidia cannot afford to lose.
articles.body: America wants to keep its most powerful AI chips out of China's hands. But China is also a market Nvidia cannot afford to lose.That contradiction has long been at the heart of the technology war between Washington and Beijing. Now, an alleged espionage scandal involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has brought the battle over AI chips into focus.Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company under scrutiny over the suspected diversion of advanced Nvidia chips to China. US intelligence assessments have reportedly raised concerns about her alleged links to Chinese intelligence — claims that remain unproven and that Beijing has rejected.Nvidia's board has launched an independent investigation into whether its CEO was targeted by foreign intelligence. The company says it has no reason to believe its secrets or US national security were compromised.But beyond the personal controversy lies a much bigger question: What makes Nvidia's AI chips so valuable that the world's two largest economies are fighting over who gets access to them?Why Nvidia's AI chips are so valuableNvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) have become central to the development and operation of modern AI systems. Unlike conventional processors, which are designed to handle a broad range of computing tasks, GPUs can perform large numbers of calculations simultaneously.This makes them particularly suited to training and running AI models, which require enormous computing power.Their importance extends beyond the technology industry. Advanced AI can be used in areas such as scientific research, industrial automation, intelligence analysis, surveillance and military applications. Governments therefore view access to high-performance chips as a matter of economic competitiveness and national security.Nvidia's advantage is not limited to the hardware itself. Its CUDA software platform allows developers to write and run applications on its GPUs. Over the years, researchers, technology companies and AI developers have built tools and systems around this ecosystem, making it difficult for rivals to replace Nvidia products without additional time, investment and engineering work.For Washington, this dominance creates considerable strategic leverage. American companies lead important areas of chip design and semiconductor technology, while US export-control rules can also restrict the supply of certain products manufactured overseas using American technology.Why the US is restricting chip sales to ChinaThe US has tightened restrictions on exports of advanced semiconductors to China since October 2022. The measures are intended to limit Beijing's access to computing power that could support advanced AI development and military capabilities.The company has developed less powerful versions of certain chips for the Chinese market in the past, but Washington has continued to adjust the rules to prevent restricted technology from reaching Chinese customers through alternative products or supply routes.Nvidia chief executive Huang has repeatedly criticised the restrictions, arguing that excluding American companies from China could strengthen local rivals.The policy has not been entirely static. In January 2026, the US Commerce Department revised its licensing approach to allow certain exports of Nvidia's H200 processors and comparable chips to China to be considered on a case-by-case basis.The permission came with conditions, including requirements relating to US supply capacity, customer compliance procedures and third-party testing in the US. It was not a blanket approval for unrestricted sales, according to the US Bureau of Industry and Security.Why China also needs Nvidia chipsChina has invested heavily in developing its own semiconductor industry, but domestic companies have yet to fully match Nvidia's capabilities across the high-end AI computing market.Data from research firm IDC, reported by Reuters, showed that Nvidia held 34% of China's data-centre AI chip market in the first half of 2026. It shipped about 678,000 AI accelerators during the period, compared with Huawei's 572,000, giving the Chinese company a 28% share.The H200 has become a particularly important point of friction. After Washington introduced a conditional licensing route for exports, Chinese authorities reportedly restricted purchases to special circumstances, such as university research. Beijing has also sought to encourage domestic companies to rely more heavily on locally developed processors.The result has been an unusual standoff. Around 600,000 Nvidia H200 processors were reportedly being held in Hong Kong while awaiting shipment to mainland China, with Beijing yet to approve large-scale imports. Some smaller shipments had reportedly been allowed through intermediaries.China's response has been to accelerate the development of domestic alternatives. Huawei is among the companies seeking to fill the gap, while other Chinese chipmakers, including Cambricon and Alibaba's T-Head, are also working to expand their presence in the market.Even so, Chinese labs still use Nvidia hardware. Omdia analyst Lian Jye Su told news agency AFP that Chinese vendors are still using cutting-edge Nvidia chips to train models.Problem of getting around US restrictionsExport controls can limit where advanced chips are shipped, but monitoring how they are ultimately used is more complicated. Companies and researchers can access computing resources through data centres in other countries, even when the end user is based in China.This creates a challenge for US authorities. A chip located in a data centre in Southeast Asia, for example, could potentially be used remotely by a customer elsewhere. The physical location of the processor does not necessarily reveal who is accessing its computing power.White House adviser Michael Kratsios recently cited the case of Chinese AI company Moonshot AI accessing high-end Nvidia processors in Thailand. Analysts have also warned that overseas data centres could provide a route around restrictions if access and end users are not adequately monitored.There have also been criminal cases involving alleged attempts to divert restricted Nvidia processors to China. In November 2025, the US Department of Justice charged four people with conspiring to illegally export Nvidia GPUs to China using false paperwork and contracts. The department alleged that the group had exported hundreds of A100 processors and attempted further shipments of H100 and H200 chips.In a separate case, businessman Alan Hao Hsu and his company, Hao Global, pleaded guilty to offences involving the export or attempted export of at least $160 million worth of Nvidia H100 and H200 processors between October 2024 and May 2025. The case involved false documentation intended to conceal the transactions.Megaspeed investigation puts Nvidia under scrutinyThe controversy surrounding Alice Huang has brought renewed attention to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company that has faced scrutiny over suspected efforts to help China obtain advanced Nvidia chips.The company's dealings have attracted attention because of its reported purchases of Nvidia processors. Reports have put the value of its purchases at about $4.8 billion over two years.Bloomberg reported that Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter contacted senior Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler in late summer 2025 to ask whether the department was involved in Singapore's detention of a Megaspeed executive. The report has raised questions about Nvidia's interactions with US officials during the investigation, but it does not establish that the company improperly interfered with the probe.Washington's divided approach to NvidiaHuang is no ordinary executive in this fight. He lobbied hard for looser chip rules, joined Trump aboard Air Force One for his May trip to Beijing, and attended the September White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trump has now defended him, calling him an "honorable guy" and saying he believed Huang did not know the woman was an alleged spy.Congress is less forgiving.Republican committee chairs John Moolenaar, Brian Mast and Rick Crawford have requested a briefing from Huang on November 18. Democratic senator Chris Coons has said he is pushing for an investigation into whether national security was compromised. Senator Elizabeth Warren has said Nvidia owes Congress answers and called for legislation to prevent advanced US technology from reaching China.Proposals such as the AI Overwatch Act seek to strengthen congressional oversight of advanced AI chip exports and establish safeguards against technology being used by military forces in countries considered adversaries. Other legislative proposals, including the Chip Security Act and the MATCH Act, have also formed part of the wider debate over semiconductor security and export controls.The issue has become part of the broader US-China diplomatic relationship. Trump is expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on November 18–19, with technology and trade among the issues shaping the wider relationship. The possibility of Huang joining the US delegation has also drawn attention amid the controversy.For Washington, restricting China's access to advanced chips is one way to preserve its lead in AI. But overly broad restrictions could also encourage Chinese companies to develop alternatives faster, potentially reducing the long-term influence of American technology firms.What the Nvidia dispute means for the global AI raceThe US has advantages in chip design, semiconductor software and access to critical manufacturing technologies. China, meanwhile, has a large domestic technology market, significant state support and an increasingly capable group of semiconductor companies. Its ability to develop alternatives will depend on how quickly it can close gaps in performance, manufacturing and software.The contest also has implications for countries caught between the two technology powers. Semiconductor manufacturing depends on a global network of companies and facilities, including advanced foundries in Taiwan. Any disruption to this supply chain could affect chipmakers, cloud-computing providers and businesses that rely on AI infrastructure around the world.That is why the dispute matters well beyond Nvidia. The company's chips have become a strategic resource in the contest for AI leadership, and the struggle over who can buy, sell and use them is increasingly shaping the relationship between the US and China.You use AI every day. articles.title: First snow, coldest air in months headed for eastern US in wake of storm
articles.summary: Winter is ready to make its first cameo of the season later this week with the coldest temps in months for millions.
articles.body: Winter will make its first cameo in the eastern United States later this week as a storm ushers in the coldest temperatures in six months for tens of millions of people and the first snow for some. 🥶 Get your local forecast and track the storm in the CNN Weather app The storm will become a nor’easter when it reaches the Northeast coast, shaking up a period of relative tranquility in the region and becoming the first notable storm since September’s early season nor’easter. Nearly 200 million people east of the Mississippi will experience their coldest temperatures since spring as a tease of winter plunges south from Canada in the storm’s wake. The storm will develop across the Midwest Wednesday and slowly strengthen as it pushes east. With it, blustery and sloppy conditions are expected from the Midwest to the Mid-Atlantic and into coastal parts of the Northeast later in the week. High elevations in the Interior Northeast are likely to see their first snowfall of fall, and the lake-effect snow machine will also power on for the first time since spring in the Great Lakes. Not every impact is locked in. How much snow and rain will impact the Northeast and New England remains in question with forecast models still disagreeing on the storm’s intensity and speed. Impacts hinge on storm’s speed Wet snow is possible in the mountains of the Interior Northeast southward through the central and southern Appalachians, especially by Thursday night and Friday. Most lower elevations, including the Interstate 95 corridor from Philadelphia to Boston, will just experience a cold rain. Some snow could mix in with rain in the valleys of the Interior Northeast. Snow totals ranging from a dusting to a few inches could coat the highest elevations of northern New England and Upstate New York. Snow is most likely to stick to the ground in the overnight hours when it’s coldest. This most likely outcome could change in two ways, depending on the storm’s speed. A quicker storm would mean less snow that sticks since it would spend less time in the cold air. The impacts would also be over a shorter duration, and most of the rain and any snow would likely be wrapped up by Saturday morning. On the other hand, a slower storm hugging the coast could allow snow to linger through Saturday. That would give it the potential to drop somewhat higher snow totals. Both storm tracks could generate gusty winds and some coastal flooding in the Northeast but will not be as severe or widespread as they were during September’s nor’easter. Whether fast, slow or somewhere in between, the storm will bring a dose of soggy weather from the Midwest to parts of the Northeast as well as a blast of cold air from the far eastern Plains to the Atlantic coast. Cold is a lock Behind the storm, a brief cold plunge is set in stone for anyone east of the Mississippi River. Many areas will see their coldest weather since last spring as temperatures drop 5 to 15 degrees Fahrenheit below average. Sub-freezing temperatures are expected in parts of the Deep South overnight Friday and Saturday. For some in the South, the first freeze may arrive right on schedule as many areas, including Atlanta and Birmingham, Alabama, typically experience it during the first half of November. Parts of central Florida, like Orlando, could dip into the 40s for the first time since March. The cold will firmly settle in over the Midwest, from Minnesota to Ohio, preventing temperatures from climbing out of the 40s starting on Thursday and lasting through the weekend. This cold snap won’t have staying power. Above-average temperatures are expected to return next week in much of the nation’s eastern half. The mild temperatures could be preview of what’s to come in a winter dominated by Super El Niño.

articles.title: Who is Jean Leonard Teganya, deported by US over Rwanda genocide claims?
articles.summary: Teganya, a former medical student, is accused of participating in the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda.
articles.body:
Jean Leonard Teganya, a former medical student accused of helping identify Tutsi civilians who were later killed during Rwanda’s 1994 genocide, has been deported from the United States to Rwanda, where he faces separate allegations of genocide and crimes against humanity.

Rwanda’s National Public Prosecution Authority (NPPA) confirmed that Teganya arrived at Kigali International Airport on the evening of November 9, 2026, accompanied by US security officers. He was handed over to Rwandan prosecutors.

The NPPA said it had indicted him in 2014 over his alleged involvement in genocide and crimes against humanity in the former Butare prefecture in southern Rwanda. It did not provide details of the specific allegations against him.

Born in 1971, Teganya was studying medicine at the National University of Rwanda in Butare during the genocide. He was also undertaking practical training at the University Teaching Hospital of Butare.

He left Rwanda in July 1994, as the genocide came to an end. According to US court records, he travelled through what was then Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as well as Kenya and India, before reaching Canada in 1999.

He applied for asylum in Canada, but his application was rejected in 2002 and again in 2012. The Canadian authorities’ decision, as described in the US appeal judgement, was based on the conclusion that he would not have survived in Rwanda in 1994 if he had not been perceived as sharing the intention to kill Tutsi and moderate Hutu.

After about 15 years of proceedings in Canada, Teganya evaded a deportation order and crossed into the United States on foot on August 3, 2014, near Houlton, Maine. He was taken into custody and applied for asylum.

The allegations against Teganya concern his conduct at the University Teaching Hospital of Butare during the genocide.

According to evidence presented by US prosecutors at his 2019 trial, Teganya was affiliated with the National Republican Movement for Democracy and Development (MRND), the ruling political party at the time, and the Interahamwe militia associated with it.

The US Department of Justice said trial evidence showed that Teganya led groups of soldiers and Interahamwe members through the hospital to search for Tutsi patients and refugees hiding there. Those discovered were taken away and killed behind the maternity ward, according to the prosecution’s account.

The prosecution also presented evidence linking him to the killing of three Tutsi people at the hospital and Tutsi students in university accommodation. It further alleged that he participated in five rapes involving two Tutsi women who had sought shelter at the hospital.

These allegations formed part of the evidence in his US immigration-related trial. They should not be confused with the specific charges in Rwanda’s separate case against him, which have not been detailed publicly.

Why was he convicted in the United States?

Teganya was not tried for genocide in the United States. The criminal case concerned statements he made to US immigration authorities.

Prosecutors accused him of concealing his political affiliations and activities during the genocide when seeking asylum.

In September 2017, he was indicted on two counts of immigration fraud and three counts of perjury. A federal jury convicted him on all five counts on April 5, 2019.

He was sentenced to 97 months in prison on July 1, 2019. The sentence included an enhancement for obstruction of justice based on his false testimony during the trial.

Teganya appealed, but the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit upheld his convictions and sentence in May 2021.

His US convictions were for immigration fraud and perjury, not genocide. The allegations about his conduct during the genocide featured in the evidence presented at trial, but the jury did not convict him of genocide.

Rwanda’s prosecution authority says it indicted Teganya in 2014 over alleged genocide and crimes against humanity committed in the former Butare prefecture.

His return allows Rwandan authorities to pursue that separate case in the country where the alleged crimes took place.

However, the NPPA’s public statement did not set out the individual allegations or specify when Teganya would appear in court. It would therefore be premature to assume that every allegation presented during his US trial forms part of the Rwandan indictment.

Teganya’s return brings him back to Rwanda to face allegations that have remained unresolved in its judicial system since 2014.

His case has crossed three legal systems: Canada’s examination of his eligibility for asylum, the US prosecution over false statements in immigration proceedings, and Rwanda’s separate allegations of genocide and crimes against humanity.

More than three decades after the genocide, the question now is whether Rwandan prosecutors can establish his individual responsibility for the crimes of which he is accused. His return does not amount to a conviction, and he will have the opportunity to defend himself in court.

articles.title: Meta’s AI age-check goes global: Can it protect teens?
articles.summary: The tech giant rolls out age-detection tool for Instagram and Facebook, but experts doubt whether it can help protect teens.
articles.body:
Meta has rolled out artificial intelligence (AI)-powered age-estimation technology worldwide in an effort to better detect teenage users who signed up for its social media platforms with an adult’s birth date.

The world’s largest social media company announced the change on Monday, saying that millions more young people worldwide would be placed in its Teen Accounts following the implementation of the new technology amid concerns that its platforms have failed to protect teenagers.

Teen Accounts have more restrictions and protections designed to provide a safer user experience. They keep the account private by default, limit content types, and prevent strangers from sending direct messages (DMs) to teenage account holders. Parents can also supervise Teen Accounts.

Experts, however, doubt whether the latest step will protect children from online harm.

Here’s what we know about the latest tool and why Meta has deployed it:

Meta, which owns Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp and Threads, said on Monday that it had started using its AI age-estimation system on Instagram accounts around the world.

“Since first introducing this technology, we’ve been placing more teens in age-appropriate protections and are encouraged by the results. Based on that success, today we’re expanding this technology globally,” the company said.

The system is designed to identify teenagers who signed up with a fake birth date in order to use a regular account. They are then switched to a restricted Teen Account or removed from the platform.

Meta is also rolling out the new age-detection tool for Facebook and plans to implement a similar system worldwide for Threads, another of its social media apps, before the end of the year.

Before Monday, the system had already been rolled out in more than 20 countries. Meta has called on competitors to adopt similar age checks.

How will age checks work, and what protections will they trigger?

Meta says its AI judges whether an account holder is likely to be a teenager, regardless of what birth date they gave when signing up.

The AI searches a user’s account to find “contextual clues” that point to their age. Examples given by Meta include “birthday celebrations or mentions of school grades”.

It also uses “visual cues” in pictures and videos on the account, but Meta says that this does not extend to facial recognition.

Flagged accounts are then moved into Teen Accounts – on Instagram, Facebook and Messenger – which limit how long teenagers can spend on the apps, which content they can access, and who they can message.

In countries that ban social media for users under a certain age, the account may be shut down entirely.

In the United States, Meta will add specific restrictions for under-18s, capping their time on its apps at two hours a day and imposing a midnight-to-6am curfew.

In Australia, the firm says it has started using an Apple feature that verifies a user’s age range when their phone is set up and passes that on to apps they download.

Meta said it supports legislation that would have app stores verify users’ ages, calling it “more effective” than having many developers devising methods to collect the information for each app.

In its announcement, Meta linked the new policy to the outcome of a groundbreaking lawsuit brought by 29 US states and cosigned by 52 US attorneys general.

The company was accused of designing Facebook and Instagram to addict children and collect their personal data, not doing enough to verify users’ ages and even encouraging minors to bypass its existing verification measures.

The suit was settled out of court in August, with Meta agreeing to pay up to $18bn to plaintiffs and to make significant changes to its platform to protect minors, including time limits, nighttime curfews and limits on filters that simulate cosmetic procedures.

Although Meta’s announcement cites the August out-of-court settlement, it has faced two other major legal actions in the US this year relating to the impact of its products on children.

In March, Meta was ordered to pay $375m when a New Mexico court found the company had been misleading about the safety of its platform for minors.

Around the same time, Meta and Google also lost a landmark case in Los Angeles, brought by a woman who said she had become addicted to Instagram and YouTube and faced mental health problems as a result.

Governments have also increasingly intervened to protect minors from what they see as the harms of social media.

In recent years, several countries have introduced social media bans for minors under a certain age, including the United Kingdom, Indonesia, Australia and Turkiye, with many more weighing similar measures.

Sonia Livingstone, a professor at the London School of Economics and director of the Digital Futures for Children Centre, told Al Jazeera that Meta had yet to deliver evidence that its system was preventing underage users from using its platforms.

She pointed to an “absence of clear evidence” that young children could not create accounts or that teenagers who use the platforms were indeed being placed in Teen Accounts.

Livingstone said that Meta’s age check system “poses a privacy risk to all users, not just children, since the point of age assurance is to figure out who the children are”.

Without independent audits to determine how it works, “it is hard to see why we should trust them with our personal data”, she said.

Although Australia banned under-16s from social media in December, its regulator, eSafety, found that more than 80 percent of preteens and young teens were still using it half a year later, largely because age checks failed to stop them.

In that same period, Meta had shut down 462,000 Instagram accounts in compliance with the ban – but eSafety found that more than 69 percent of underage users retained their Instagram accounts.

There is also the risk that teenage users simply migrate to another platform that contains similar risks to their health.

Under the $18bn August settlement, about $5bn of Meta’s payment is conditional on its competitors, including TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat, agreeing to similar measures and payments.

Many of these platforms are also facing regulatory heat for similar issues to Meta. On Friday, European Union regulators threatened to fine TikTok owner ByteDance 6 percent of its global annual revenue for its addictive design.

EU tech commissioner Henna Virkunnen said the platform was “leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from” and called on TikTok to “step up its efforts to protect users’ wellbeing, including those of minors”.

articles.title: Faced with influx, prosecutor in Washington says he lacks resources to defend immigration cases
articles.summary: Judges have often ruled against the administration in cases filed by tens of thousands of detainees arguing that they were being held illegally by ICE.
articles.body: TACOMA, Wash. (AP) — Faced with an influx of petitions by people alleging they’re being unlawfully detained by federal immigration authorities, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Washington said Monday that it no longer has the staffing to defend every case and will let judges rule without government opposition. Acting U.S. Attorney Charles Floyd said in a letter to U.S. District Judge David Estudillo that habeas corpus cases initiate “protracted litigation” with numerous hearings, briefings and motions that consume prosecutors’ resources. “Thus, going forward, in order to conserve resources, there will be many habeas cases in which the USAO will no longer assume responsibility for providing a defense on behalf of the respondents,” Floyd wrote. The backlog has “severely impacted the government’s ability to respond” to immigration petitions and prevented prosecutors from dealing with other unrelated civil litigation, he said. As a result, his office will decline to defend “many” habeas cases. He didn’t specify how many cases could be affected. Judges have often ruled against the administration in cases filed by tens of thousands of detainees arguing that they were being held illegally by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. It has been a source of great frustration to administration officials — and to judges and advocates who say ICE has trampled on individual rights amid the Trump administration’s hardline immigration agenda. Last week, U.S. border czar Tom Homan told Fox News that courts have been weighed down by about 85,000 immigration habeas cases as the government carries out a sweeping crackdown. Floyd is a former judge who, along with three other Washington judges, advocated for prohibiting immigration courts from granting bond to detainees — a question that is now before the U.S. Supreme Court. The justices will consider whether immigrants who have been living in the U.S. have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation. Most appeals courts to have considered the issue have found that it violates federal law to detain immigrants, including those living in the U.S. illegally, without a bond hearing. Those decisions conflict with rulings by the 5th and 8th circuits, which held that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the U.S. must be detained while their deportation cases are pending.

articles.title: Israel govt formation: Netanyahu in 'panic' as Eisenkot-led bloc agree on key Knesset positions
articles.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu is gripped by \"panic\" over the possibility of opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot ousting him as Prime Minister, former Bibi adviser Nir
articles.body: Benjamin Netanyahu is gripped by "panic" over the possibility of opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot ousting him as Prime Minister, former Bibi adviser Nir Hefetz claimed on Tuesday during an interview with 103FM."Panic is a major factor in his decision-making," Hefetz said, according to The Jerusalem Post. "I could almost close my eyes and hear that atmosphere of panic," he added.Speaking about the atmosphere in the Prime Minister's Office during periods of political uncertainty, Hefetz claimed that urgent calls from Netanyahu's wife, Sara, and son, Yair, were frequent."Urgent phone calls every five seconds with the same message from Yair and Sara," he said, referring to people around Netanyahu including "Qatar's representatives in the office or people like [Knesset Speaker] Amir Ohana.""If you were a fly on the wall, you would see the panic with your own eyes," Hefetz said. "This is not unusual for him when his personal standing is at risk. It is a regular feature of how he operates when it comes to himself."Hefetz says Netanyahu fears losing powerHefetz said losing office would be particularly difficult for Netanyahu and his family, pointing to the status and privileges associated with being prime minister."Life at home would not be easy for him, to put it mildly. And don't forget, he is someone who loves the respect he receives from world leaders," he said."Will he sit on the opposition benches? Will he suddenly see Eisenkot with the motorcade, being taken everywhere by helicopter and flying on Wing of Zion?" he asked, referring to Israel's official state aircraft."That triumvirate of Netanyahu, Sara and Yair would simply explode. For them, it would be worse than people being abducted to Gaza," Hefetz claimed.He also suggested that Netanyahu's call for a national unity government could be a political move to slow Eisenkot's efforts to form an alternative administration."The closer Gadi Eisenkot gets to forming a government, the less Netanyahu will be willing to settle for," Hefetz said, suggesting that the prime minister could offer further concessions to prevent Eisenkot from taking office."The moment Eisenkot enters negotiations with him over a unity government, it becomes less urgent. But first, he needs to stop the snowball," he added.Hefetz argued that Netanyahu was also keen to preserve his longstanding alliance with the ultra-Orthodox parties, whose support could determine who commands a parliamentary majority.Eisenkot received mandate to form next govtThe remarks came as Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, secured an agreement with four opposition leaders on key positions in the Knesset, strengthening their efforts to replace Netanyahu and form the next government.The agreement was reached with Naftali Bennett, Yair Golan, Avigdor Liberman and Yair Lapid. The leaders have nominated former minister Matan Kahana, a member of Eisenkot's Yashar party, as their candidate for Speaker of the Knesset.Liberman will head the powerful Foreign affairs and defence committee, while incoming lawmaker Liran Avisar Ben Horin of Bennett's B'Yachad party has been nominated to chair the Finance Committee. She would become the first woman to hold the post.Incoming lawmaker Roy Folkman has been nominated to head the House Committee. The parties have also agreed to establish special committees, with details to be announced separately.Earlier anouncing the decision, in a post on X, Eisenkot said, "I have reached an agreement with my partners, the leaders of the change and reform parties--Naftali Bennett, Yair Golan, Avigdor Liberman, and Yair Lapid--on the prospective candidates for key positions in the 26th Knesset during the period for forming a government.""Speaker of the Knesset--former minister and incoming MK Matan Kahana," he added.Netanyahu's governing bloc won 53 seats in the 120-member legislature, while the Zionist opposition parties secured 48. Arab-led parties hold the remaining 19 seats.Eisenkot received the mandate to form the next government from President Isaac Herzog on Sunday after securing recommendations from lawmakers representing 67 seats, compared with 46 for Netanyahu.The backing included support from Arab lawmakers, although most leaders of the Zionist opposition parties have ruled out including Arab parties in a government.Eisenkot has 28 days to form a government, with a possible two-week extension. The ultra-Orthodox parties, which hold 13 seats and have traditionally been Netanyahu's allies, could prove crucial to the coalition negotiations.Hefetz: Bibi knows Eisenkot is not afraid of himComparing Eisenkot with former prime minister Naftali Bennett, Hefetz argued that Netanyahu viewed the former IDF chief of staff as a more formidable political opponent."Even during the first months when Naftali was prime minister, Netanyahu was in a terrible mood," Hefetz said. "But there is an enormous difference between Gadi Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett.""Netanyahu knows this very well. Eisenkot is not afraid of him, and he knows he cannot mess with Eisenkot," he added."He won't stammer 'Yonit, Yonit,' and Idit Silman won't suddenly walk out on him," Hefetz said, referring to Bennett's political difficulties and the defection of Silman from his coalition in 2022.Hefetz also cited comments by former minister Elazar Stern, who recalled Eisenkot saying that his experiences during the war had changed his perspective on political pressure."Gadi told me, 'After everything I went through in the last war, nothing can touch me,'" Hefetz quoted Stern as saying. "And Bibi knows that."Hefetz argued that Eisenkot's reputation and personal credibility could help him secure support from potential coalition partners, particularly ultra-Orthodox parties."That is also his main weapon in forming a government," Hefetz said. "If Eisenkot, with the reputation he has, tells the ultra-Orthodox parties, 'You have my word that this is what will happen, and it will stay in this room,' they can rely on that."He also suggested that Yisrael Beytenu leader Liberman's recent political positions could reflect private understandings with Eisenkot.Netanyahu's corruption trial could be affectedHefetz also discussed the possible implications of Netanyahu losing office for his ongoing corruption trial.He suggested that the prime minister's current position had influenced the court's handling of his schedule and that judges could impose stricter attendance requirements if he moved to the opposition."Have you considered how much his life would change?" Hefetz asked. "The panel of judges sitting in the District Court, which allows Amit Hadad to run the proceedings, will tell him: 'You will attend every hearing.'""The judges will take control, and he will sit there day after day," Hefetz added.You use AI every day. articles.title: What is Shahid Kaveh, ⁠⁠the Iran cyberunit tied to France’s fridge hacking?
articles.summary: IRGC-linked unit operates through front groups posing as vigilante hackers to hit adversaries, says French intelligence.
articles.body:
The French government has accused Shahid Kaveh – a group it says is linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) – of being behind recent cyberattacks targeting refrigerators in French supermarkets.

The alleged sabotage campaign last month hacked into refrigeration systems in hundreds of stores in France and remotely cranked up temperatures, spoiling millions of euros’ worth of food.

France’s Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot has called the attack “unprecedented in its level of aggression”.

But in a statement on Tuesday, Iran denied any role in the cyberattacks.

Here’s what we know about Shahid Kevah and its alleged involvement:

French officials have accused the IRGC of orchestrating the October 11-12 cyberattack, which they say targeted 700 commercial sites across France.

In a statement, the Paris prosecutor’s office specifically blamed Shahid Kaveh, which it described as a “an offensive cyberunit” affiliated with the IRGC’s cyberelectronic command (CEC).

A report published by France’s spy and cyberagencies also named three alleged perpetrators – Hamid Reza Lashgarian, who it described as the head of the CEC, and Mahdi Lashgarian and Reza Salarvand, who it identified as commanders in the Shahid Kaveh unit.

Iran pushed back against the accusations on Tuesday, calling them “baseless and biased”.

The Iranian Foreign Ministry, in a statement, described the accusations as a “highly irresponsible and contemptible action to tarnish Iran’s image and disrupt its relations with other countries”.

The statement warned that Tehran would not hesitate to take measures to safeguard its national interests and security.

It made no mention of the Shahid Kaveh unit.

Iran’s government has never publicly acknowledged the existence or purpose of the group, which appears to be named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an IRGC commander who died aged 25 in 1986 during the Iran-Iraq war.

But Western intelligence agencies have linked it to the IRGC, assessing that it is part of a network of hackers operating under Tehran’s direction.

In their recent report, French spy and cyber agencies said Shahid Kaveh operates through numerous front groups posing as vigilante hackers, including “CyberAveng3rs” and “Cyber Isnaad Front.”

Those front groups, it said, “are tasked with publicly claiming responsibility for certain attacks carried out by the Shahid Kaveh unit”.

Two of the alleged associates named by French intelligence agencies – Hamid Reza Lashgarian and Mahdi Lashgarian – have previously been sanctioned by the US over alleged ties to the IRGC’s cyberunit.

What do we know about Iran’s cyberattack capabilities?

Iran has extensive cybercapabilities that it is increasingly using to advance its wartime objectives, say experts.

Nikita Shah, a senior fellow with the Intelligence, National Security, and Technology programme at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), says there has been a “notable uptick in Iran’s cyberoperations since March 2026”, including “cyberespionage” and “conflict-themed cybercrime”.

“Iran’s cyberoperators will likely be working on preparing new technical accesses, and possibly new cyber capabilities to leverage, should the conflict continue over the longer term or negotiations falter,” Shah wrote in an August analysis for CSIS.

A 2025 policy report by the United Kingdom Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee describes Iran as “an aggressive cyberactor with extensive capabilities”.

While Iran’s cybercapacity is not as sophisticated as Russia’s or China’s, according to the report, Tehran is adept at using basic exploitation methods against its adversaries.

“Whilst Iranian cyberactors often use simple computer network exploitation techniques, they use them very effectively, exploiting basic vulnerabilities that many organisations have, including in the UK,” said the report.

Cyberoperations are also a “deniable tool” that Iran can use to “attack its enemies, respond to perceived aggression and project power in the region – and globally,” the report added.

Other than France, who else has been targeted?

The IRGC and affiliated groups have been linked to past cyberattacks on targets in the United States and Israel, including water infrastructure.

One wave of attacks in late 2023 targeted US water facilities that relied on a computer system made by Israeli software firm Unitronics, according to US cybersecurity officials.

Earlier this year, Iran-affiliated hackers also went after industrial control technology used in US infrastructure, including at government facilities, US security agencies warned. The hackers were able to disrupt some programmable logic controllers (PLCs) — technology that helps automate and monitor machinery and manufacturing processes — across several US critical infrastructure sectors, causing “operational disruption and financial loss”, the US agencies said.

And in March this year, an Iran-linked hacking group claimed to carry out a destructive cyberattack on US-based medical device provider, Stryker.

The recent French intelligence report said attacks by Shahid Kaveh and its affiliated groups have been “primarily directed against Israel and the United States, but also against France and other European countries”.

articles.title: Viktor Orban’s brother detained in people-smuggling case, Hungary’s PM says
articles.summary: Hungary has detained the brother of former Prime Minister ​Viktor Orban during its investigation of a people-smuggling case, Prime Minister Peter Magyar confirmed during a speech in Berlin.
articles.body: Hungary has detained the brother of former Prime Minister ​Viktor Orban during its investigation of a people-smuggling case, Prime Minister Peter Magyar confirmed during a speech in Berlin. Monday’s comments came after the Hungarian anti-graft body, said in a statement it and ⁠police had detained four people and searched homes at several sites in Budapest and Pest county as part of the case. “Three out of the ex-ministers of Orban are already in custody,” Magyar said on the sidelines of a speech in ⁠the German capital. “Already his brother today went ​to ⁠custody,” he added, referring to the former prime minister’s sibling, businessman Aron Orban, 49. Writing on Facebook, Viktor Orban dismissed his brother’s detention as ⁠an instance of political revenge. “In this dirty game, the aim ​is ⁠the elimination of the political opponent ‌and the establishment of a one-party system. I am the target, my younger brother is just a tool,” the former prime minister wrote. In Monday’s ‌statement, the National Asset Protection and Recovery Office ‌did not identify the suspects detained and police also declined to do so in an emailed response to Reuters. The body was set up to investigate allegations of corruption during ⁠Orban’s 16-year rule, which the latter has denied. It was established by Magyar, who ousted Orban in an April election, and is central to his government’s anti-graft campaign which he has dubbed “Operation Purgatory”. Monday’s statement had said the four detained were suspected of helping Vietnamese citizens reach Western Europe for several months in 2024. The perpetrators charged visa applicants a so-called recruitment fee at ‌Hungary’s foreign missions in Vietnam, which they then shared, the authorities ​said. The woman and three men held are suspected “of human smuggling ‌committed as part of a ⁠criminal conspiracy for the purpose of financial gain,” police said. In September, ⁠the NVVH said “selling political connections to obtain residence permits for employment.” was among the first four ‌cases it planned ​to investigate. Two former ministers from Orban’s ‌government and former central bank chief Gyorgy ​Matolcsy are currently under arrest over graft accusations in separate investigations.

articles.title: Trump’s Board of Peace chides Israel for ‘insufficient’ response to Gaza flooding
articles.summary: The Board of Peace urged Israel to allow essential aid into Gaza, after calling its response to massive weekend flooding across the shattered enclave “insufficient.”
articles.body: US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace urged Israel to allow essential aid into Gaza, after calling its response to massive weekend flooding across the shattered enclave “insufficient.” Seasonal rains swamped tens of thousands of tents across Gaza, where nearly 2 million Palestinians are displaced, according to the United Nations. “The urgent entry and distribution of essential shelter, sanitation, drainage, and other winterization supplies is critical to protecting civilian lives,” the Board of Peace said in a statement Monday. Created by the Trump administration and backed by a UN Security Council resolution, the organization was supposed to oversee implementation of a Gaza ceasefire signed a year ago, and the reconstruction of the enclave, but the effort has stalled for months. The Board of Peace called on Israel to “authorize the entry of essential materials for temporary shelter, water and sanitation infrastructure, waste management, drainage, and sewage removal.” Much of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure has been destroyed in Israel’s bombardment of the territory during three years of war. The Israeli prime minister’s office said Tuesday that Israel would “continue to support winter preparedness in Gaza,” pointing to other humanitarian supplies it said had entered the enclave. “Israel and the Board of Peace face a common challenge,” the statement said, adding that “as long as Hamas remains in power, it will use every dual-use item entering Gaza to entrench its terror regime and expand its military arsenal.” Since the nominal ceasefire went into effect in October 2025, Israel’s near-daily strikes have killed more than 1,400 people in Gaza, according to the UN, and no hospitals in the enclave are fully functioning. Philippe Lazzarini, the former head of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA), described the board’s assessment of the Israeli response to the floods as an “understatement.” Lazzarini noted its “rare recognition” that Israel is not doing enough to address the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, then slammed the board – which largely avoids harsh criticism of the Israeli government – saying “it does not use any of its leverage to address the disgraceful dystopian misery of the Palestinians in Gaza.” On Sunday evening, a sand embankment in Deir al-Balah collapsed on the tents of displaced Palestinians after heavy rains, killing three children and one woman, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who led a multinational effort to impose sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, warned, “The humanitarian situation in Gaza is getting worse. Heavy rain. Flooded tents. The reality on the ground is heartbreaking.” “The UK government will not standby. We will not rest until we bring an end to the intolerable suffering,” he said in a statement on X. On Sunday, Israel said that more than 91,000 tents had entered Gaza ahead of winter, but it will not allow in the heavy equipment required for large-scale cleanup and rubble removal efforts. “The reconstruction of Gaza can only begin after Hamas fully disarms,” said Israel’s Coordinator for Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), which oversees Gaza. “Israel will not permit the entry of equipment that could be used to develop terrorist capabilities.”

articles.title: Why is India trying to broker a Russia-Ukraine Black Sea food corridor?
articles.summary: India has influence with both sides, but shipping security and Russia’s cooperation remain major obstacles.
articles.body:
India is ready to help broker “food corridors” through the Black Sea, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after a phone call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday.

The announcement came on the eve of United States-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi , with Russia and Ukraine returning to the negotiating table after a nine-month pause.

Hours later, India’s External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar spoke with his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.

Russia and Ukraine have attacked one another’s ports this year, choking off grain and oilseed exports that feed import-dependent countries in Africa and South Asia, and leaving India short of sunflower oil.

What is India offering, why does it want the role, and can it deliver?

“India is ready to mediate in establishing food corridors, and we are counting on these efforts to continue,” Zelenskyy posted on X after the call. The leaders discussed Russia’s blocking of grain exports in the Black Sea, he said.

Modi did not mention food corridors or the Black Sea, but reaffirmed India’s commitment to contributing “in every possible way” towards a peaceful resolution.

Jaishankar said his call with Lavrov focused on the war and “ongoing diplomatic initiatives”.

While New Delhi has not published a formal plan, the offer builds on proposals Indian officials floated for weeks.

During a visit to Kyiv in September, Jaishankar reportedly spoke of a potential pause on strikes against Black Sea shipping and energy infrastructure. On October 4, he said India was talking to both Russia and Ukraine about shipping safety, grain and energy exports and “non-attack possibilities”.

“India has become quietly proactive of late,” Praveen Donthi, senior India analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera.

Previously, India was “reticent … regarding a mediation role” and limited to “rhetorical calls for diplomacy and dialogue”, he added. Jaishankar’s September visit was a sign of stepping up, he said.

By early October, Kyiv received four ceasefire proposals from India, Turkiye, Egypt and the US.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called India’s proposal “the broadest”, because it covers both the Black Sea and energy infrastructure. The US plan offers only a halt to strikes on energy facilities.

Kyiv says it will accept an energy and Black Sea truce only if the two come together. Russia has so far rejected partial ceasefires, insisting on a comprehensive peace agreement instead.

Ravi Joshi, a visiting fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi and former civil servant, told DD India that “an immediate understanding or a ceasefire is important, and that’s what India can talk about”.

He added that insurance remains a current challenge.

“The ships are not being adequately insured. The insurers are not guaranteeing the safety of the ships,” he said.

The Black Sea tensions cost India directly.

On November 3, the Ministry of External Affairs said five Indian nationals had been killed in attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea and two more had gone missing.

India is also the world’s biggest importer of vegetable oils and buys most of its sunflower oil from Russia and Ukraine. Its edible oil imports fell 7 percent in September.

Sunflower oil imports fell to 108,837 tonnes that month, the lowest since April 2022, the Reuters news agency reported. In October, a 20,000-tonne Russian cargo bound for India was cancelled because of damage to port infrastructure, and about 60,000 tonnes more were delayed.

“For India, this is a priority because this has caused fluctuations in grain prices and increases. So there’s an alignment there,” Maximilian Hess, a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, told Al Jazeera.

According to Donthi, of the International Crisis Group, US President Donald Trump “has accused India of funding the Russian war efforts for buying Russian oil “.

“By mediating in the war, with some concrete proposals, India stands to gain geopolitical heft and credibility that might blunt some of the unwarranted criticism it received in the recent past,” Donthi said, adding: “It will add to its global prestige after having lost some sheen in the past year.”

Before Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, about a third of the world’s grain exports passed through the Black Sea, with Ukraine supplying a tenth of global wheat exports and 15 percent of maize, Al Jazeera has reported .

Disruption hits food-importing countries hardest, particularly in Africa and parts of Asia.

This year, the Black Sea has turned into a two-way port war.

Russia has intensified strikes on Ukraine’s Odesa ports, which normally handle about 90 percent of its grain shipments, while Ukraine has hit Russian grain terminals.

In August, Ukraine’s Ministry of Agriculture cut its forecast for 2026-27 agricultural exports by more than half, to about 29.6 million tonnes, RBC-Ukraine reported . By mid-August, attacks on shipping had shut down more than 97 percent of Russia and Ukraine’s grain export capacity in the Azov and Black Sea basin, according to Reuters.

The last deal of this kind, the United Nations- and Turkiye-brokered Black Sea Grain Initiative, allowed nearly 33 million tonnes of food to leave three Ukrainian ports from July 2022, before Russia withdrew a year later.

India is one of few major powers with working relationships in both Moscow and Kyiv.

Joshi said India’s strategic autonomy puts it in a position to push for peace because New Delhi is “friends with both” sides.

In July, it summoned Moscow’s charge d’affaires to condemn a Russian strike on a merchant vessel that killed 10 people, including four Indian crew members. Days later, it summoned Ukraine’s ambassador over an Indian seafarer killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the MV Omorfi, PTI reported.

In the 2025-26 marketing year, India imported 1.46 million tonnes of sunflower oil from Russia and 443,000 tonnes from Ukraine, according to the Indian Solvent Extractors’ Association (SEA), alongside large volumes of Russian crude.

Hess, at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said Zelenskyy approached India “because they have leverage over Moscow, and they are one of the few major buyers of its oil still”.

He added that a large amount of Russian money sits in the Indian financial system, which Moscow wants to keep access to.

For a start, New Delhi has not publicly confirmed the offer. Modi only spoke of contributing to a peaceful resolution, leaving India’s commitment in question.

Kyiv also has doubts about India’s neutrality. Ukraine has repeatedly pressed New Delhi over its purchases of Russian oil, which Jaishankar defended during his September visit, saying they would not determine the course of the war.

Hess said Zelenskyy “wants to show India that it should perhaps revisit the state of its partnership with Moscow”.

“It’s important for Ukraine to show everybody that Russia isn’t a trustworthy partner,” he said.

The 2022 grain deal relied on Turkiye, which controls access to the Black Sea through the Bosphorus and hosted the deal’s joint inspection centre in Istanbul. Any new corridor would need ships, insurers and inspections that India cannot supply alone.

Turkiye, Egypt and the US have all tabled proposals, and the Kremlin says the Abu Dhabi talks are trilateral, with Washington as the sole mediator.

Above all, a corridor would now require both sides to stop. Unlike in 2022, Ukraine is also striking Russian grain terminals. Russia, for its part, walked away from the last grain deal in 2023.

Hess said earlier attempts towards a standalone corridor failed “because Russia kept attacking Ukrainian ports”, and that shipping recovered only when Ukraine used naval drones to push Russia’s fleet away.

Russian and Ukrainian delegations are meeting in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, but talks are stuck on the issue of territory – something that is “impossible to negotiate”, said Joshi.

Hess added, “Russia has yet to offer any concessions and has, in fact, increased its own demands in places. The negotiations and these offers have alternate aims other than an actual deal, but rather to affect the thinking and the positioning of other countries.”

With troop casualty numbers at record highs, Moscow is likely to be facing pressure domestically, he said.

“Russia’s entire purpose of engaging in negotiations with Europe and the United States is to divide and conquer,” Hess said. “For the Russians, [it is] about trying to make the Ukrainians take the blame. For the Ukrainians, it’s about trying to make others see the Russians as acting in bad faith.”

(Al Jazeera)

articles.title: James D. Sinegal was a grocery bagger at San Diego’s FedMart; he rose through retail and co-founded Costco in 1983
articles.summary: Discover the inspiring journey of James D. Sinegal from grocery bagger to co-founder of Costco, and how his innovative management strategies transformed retail, ensuring high employee welfare and low prices for consumers.
articles.body: Before he became a name inseparable from the history of Costco, James D. Sinegal worked a job stocking shelves at a discount store. This job became an early training ground for Sinegal on his path to co-founding Costco. It all started back in 1954, when he entered San Diego Junior College and began working at FedMart. He would eventually climb up the ladder, from grocery bagger to executive vice president, before joining Seattle retailer Jeff Brotman to establish Costco in 1983.His early career went from FedMart to working in the capacity of executive roles at various companies, a chronology traced by the University of Portland. According to the California Community Colleges Chancellor’s Office, Sinegal attended San Diego Junior College, which was later renamed San Diego City College, before he transferred to San Diego State University. His college experience revived his interest in education after high school. For this, Sinegal tipped his hat to the community college system for the opportunity to continue his education.The blueprint of a retail giantSinegal’s rise through the ranks of FedMart went beyond the scope of store-floor work. He served as the executive vice president at the helm of merchandising and operations. According to the California Community Colleges Chancellor’s Office, the same office lists his next move as vice president from 1977 to 1978. He became the executive vice president of the Price Company from 1978 to 1979. Between 1979 and 1983, he worked at Sinegal/Chamberlain and Associates as a broker and sales representative for food and non-food products.Sol Price was Sinegal’s principal mentor and a major influence on his career. Working for Price left a lasting impression on Sinegal; he had wanted to pursue law but chose business after several months at FedMart. He said: “I wanted to be like Sol Price”.Sinegal and Brotman founded Costco in Seattle in 1983. Their launch strategy hinged on a radical premise: strip retail down to its bare bones by cost-cutting. As per the University of Portland, they removed store fittings, large sales teams, the delivery system, advertising and reserve inventory. Sinegal also imposed a 14% ceiling on mark-ups for national brands, a policy intended to keep prices low for members, the University of Portland noted.Sinegal’s innovative decision-making would make Costco one of the first warehouse clubs to include fresh food, eye-care clinics, pharmacies and petrol stations, according to the Chancellor’s Office. In 1993, Costco merged with Price Club, founded by Sol Price, and became PriceCostco. Price would leave the company in 1994. The business became Costco Companies in 1997, and Price Club stores were rebranded. It became Costco Wholesale in 1999.Higher wages and a people-first management style Sinegal’s approach to staffing became part of Costco’s management model. He visited stores and kept tabs on customer comments. For Sinegal, employees’ welfare was non-negotiable, so he put them ahead of shareholders. He believed that higher wages helped retain workers and support the communities where Costco operated. Sinegal worked without any executive pretence, led by example, wore a simple name tag that read “JIM”, answered his own telephone, and sometimes stocked shelves himself.According to a 2024 Harvard Business School article, Costco reportedly paid $26 an hour, compared to other retailers that paid $17. Costco’s employee turnover rate was 8%, compared to 60% at other retailers. Singel himself followed the company’s management model and took an annual salary of $350,000 for many years. A modest number compared with what chief executives at Fortune 100 companies took close to $1million.Moreover, around 90% of Costco employees qualified for employer-sponsored health insurance. According to an Inc. report in 2026, Sinegal stepped down as Costco chief executive in 2011, after 28 years. He remained on Costco’s board until 2018. The California Community Colleges Chancellor’s office records his retirement as taking effect on 31 December 2011. San Diego State University profile also reported that he continued as a company advisor and served as an executive in residence at its Fowler College of Business. He also volunteered on the University’s Campanile Foundation Board and Fowler College of Business Advisory Board.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Poland gunman fascinated by Norway’s neo-Nazi mass killer Breivik
articles.summary: Suspect in deadly November 7 Krakow shooting looked up the white supremacist who killed dozens in 2011, a minister says.
articles.body:
A Polish man who opened fire in Krakow city’s main square and killed six people on Saturday visited websites about Norwegian white-supremacist killer Anders Behring Breivik , according to Poland’s justice minister.

Waldemar Zurek said on Tuesday that there was “a very strong indication of right-wing extremism” behind the gunman’s actions that shook the nation on November 7 .

Investigators also found in his possessions a Gadsden flag – a US Civil War-era flag featuring a rattlesnake on a yellow background that is often linked to the US far right, the minister added.

Prosecutors named the suspect as 24-year-old factory worker Michal Oksinski . He died in hospital on Monday after being shot and arrested by police minutes after they said he opened fire from his car in Krakow’s historic main square, a popular tourist destination.

Zurek said that a silencer, a muzzle device used to reduce the noise of a gun, was found in the car used by the killer.

The bodies of Oksinski’s father, mother and sister were found in their family home on Saturday. Officials say they were also likely killed by Oksinski.

In July 2011, anti-Muslim neo-Nazi Breivik killed eight people with a car bomb in Oslo and then shot and killed 69 others, most of them teenagers, at a Labour Party youth camp on Utoeya island.

The suspect’s motives have been the subject of a bitter political dispute since Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said on Saturday, just hours after the incident, that he had been influenced by far-right ideology.

Nationalist opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski called Kierwinski’s statement a “blatant lie” and members of the government appeared to backtrack on Monday.

Right-wing PiS lawmaker Michal Wojcik told the Reuters news agency that he was “outraged” by Justice Minister Zurek’s comments. “In my view, representatives of the Polish government are acting dishonestly toward the international community,” he said.

Kierwinski told public radio on Tuesday that he was not taking back anything he had said but that he was waiting to see investigators’ findings.
