articles.title: Man charged with murder on cruise that left Texas says he ‘snapped’ and choked woman, complaint says
articles.summary: A man seen on video being escorted off a cruise ship in Texas after a woman’s body was found in a cabin room told authorities that he repeatedly struck and choked her after they got into an argument, according to a criminal complaint.
articles.body: A man seen on video being escorted off a cruise ship in Texas after a woman’s body was found in a cabin room told authorities that he repeatedly struck and choked her after they got into an argument, according to a criminal complaint. Jason Leon Watford, 48, was charged with murder in connection with the investigation involving the MSC Seascape, according to the complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas. Jail records show he was in the Galveston County Jail on a federal hold Monday evening. He appeared in court for an initial hearing Tuesday afternoon and is due back in court on Monday for a probable cause hearing. The victim has not been identified, and it’s unclear whether Watford has retained an attorney. The Galveston medical examiner’s office said Monday that the deceased was a female and that an autopsy is scheduled for Tuesday. Authorities believe the woman was killed Sunday night. She was found lying on the floor of the room and had “multiple facial injuries,” the complaint says. Watford told the FBI in an interview that he and the woman got into an argument while eating dinner at a restaurant on the ship, according to the complaint. He alleged that they continued to argue after they returned to their room, causing him to “snap” and hit her multiple times, the complaint says. According to the complaint, Watford said at one point he choked the woman and wrapped his arm around her neck while she was lying down. He said that he applied pressure to her neck for about four to five minutes and “released his hold only after becoming exhausted,” the complaint says. The complaint states that a security camera showed Watford returning to the room at 7:46 p.m. ET and the woman arriving at 8:11 p.m. ET. No one else was seen entering the room. Watford said the woman was lying motionless on the floor for about 10 minutes before a housekeeper knocked on the door, the complaint says. The complaint says the footage showed the housekeeper knocking at 9:02 p.m. ET to provide towels. Watford opened the door and briefly spoke to the housekeeper, the complaint says. After the housekeeper left, Watford exited the room wearing different clothes, sat on the hallway floor and scrolled on his phone, the complaint says. Employees of the ship later responded to the room after the housekeeper reported seeing blood on Watford’s hands and pants and “a motionless female lying face down on the floor,” the complaint states. He was detained by ship security, and authorities were called. The FBI said that during a search of the room, they found bloodstained clothing on the floor. Jail records show that Watford was arrested in 2024 on a charge of assault causing bodily injury to a family member. He was sentenced to 15 months of probation and 30 hours of community service. The 1,060-foot cruise ship left Galveston on Sunday but was instructed to turn around after what the ship company described in a statement as a “guest incident aboard our ship.” The ship was scheduled to travel to Costa Maya, the Roatan Islands and Cozumel before returning to Texas on Nov. 15. Passenger Becsei György told NBC News that late Sunday night, an announcement said, “Mike Echo at level 10.” On Monday morning, he awoke to find that the ship had returned to Galveston.

articles.title: First day of Ukraine peace talks sparks hope, but Donetsk and Nato's role remain hurdles
articles.summary: The first day of Ukraine, Russia and US peace talks ended with Washington claiming progress towards ending the war, but the biggest obstacles to a
articles.body: The first day of Ukraine, Russia and US peace talks ended with Washington claiming progress towards ending the war, but the biggest obstacles to a settlement remain firmly in place.US secretary of state Marco Rubio described the four-hour discussions in Abu Dhabi as "very productive", while disagreements over control of Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region, postwar security guarantees and Nato's role continue to cast doubt on the prospects of a breakthrough.According to a BBC report, senior officials from the three countries are scheduled to reconvene on Wednesday for a second round of discussions. While Ukrainian and Russian representatives remained tight-lipped after the first day's negotiations, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner told delegates that Washington had "narrowed the gaps" between Moscow and Kyiv and hoped to move towards a "solution that hopefully ends the war".Kushner and US special envoy Steve Witkoff are leading Washington's diplomatic push in Abu Dhabi, with the discussions focused on addressing the postwar security concerns of both Russia and Ukraine.Kushner said the negotiations were aimed at building a path towards ending the conflict, while US officials indicated that both sides had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately" on the question of territorial control. However, the precise nature of any movement in their positions has not been disclosed.A central issue in the negotiations is the future of Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region, where Russia has occupied large areas but Ukrainian forces continue to hold some territory.Moscow has demanded that Kyiv surrender the remaining parts of the region under its control, while Ukraine wants the existing frontline to be frozen, allowing it to retain those areas. According to the BBC, neither side has publicly shifted from its position, making the territorial dispute one of the biggest obstacles to a peace agreement.The territorial deadlock is closely linked to another major sticking point, the postwar security arrangements for both countries. A US official told the BBC that the Donetsk dispute cannot be resolved without first determining the security framework that would follow a peace agreement."They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said, adding that neither issue could be finalised independently of the other.The proposed security framework could include assurances for Ukraine that its allies would come to its aid in the event of another Russian attack, while Moscow continues to seek limits on Nato's presence in Eastern Europe.According to the BBC, US officials have discussed security consultations, crisis communication hotlines and "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two sides. They have also floated the possibility of reactivating the Nato-Russia Council, which has remained largely inactive since 2022.Another point of contention is the role of European countries in the peace process, with leaders across the continent pushing for a place at the negotiating table after being largely excluded from previous discussions.Their concerns stem from the possibility that decisions affecting Europe's long-term security could be taken without their participation. Acknowledging their importance, Rubio said during a visit to Paris that the Europeans "are a part of solving this problem for the long term".However, a US official told the BBC that Moscow remains reluctant to involve European governments, saying the Russians "have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans".Russia has also rejected calls for an unconditional ceasefire before negotiations, arguing that it would give Ukrainian forces time to regroup.Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov reiterated Moscow's opposition to the proposal on Tuesday, saying, "We will not agree to it." The rejection highlights another divide between Russia and several European governments, which have pushed for a ceasefire as a prerequisite for broader peace negotiations.Meanwhile, concerns over the direction of Trump's peace initiative have also emerged in Kyiv, where some political leaders fear Washington could push for a quick settlement at Ukraine's expense.Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, who heads the parliamentary committee on foreign affairs, told the BBC that he believed Trump wanted "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", an outcome he said Kyiv would reject.He argued that Russian President Vladimir Putin would have little incentive to negotiate seriously as long as Moscow's military campaign continued.You use AI every day. articles.title: America's veterans and military heroes deserve far more recognition than they get: YouTube star
articles.summary: YouTube star Nic Flood says young people today know far more about pop stars than they do America's military and veteran heroes. His new book series, "Heroes Erased," aims to change that.
articles.body: A former Army National Guard medic and YouTube star based in Iowa with several million followers has a message for Veterans Day and beyond. Nic Flood, a journeyman electrician and father of two, told Fox News Digital that when people "learn about America’s war heroes, you’re learning about some of the best, bravest individuals that have ever existed on the face of the planet. And if you can draw from those experiences and learn those lessons, it’s going to help you in life." Flood has built an online following by telling the stories of American military heroes, from their childhood to their service and on through their later-in-life experiences. HIDDEN CAUSE OF VETERANS' STRUGGLES DRIVES RENEWED URGENCY IN VA MESSAGING "If you forget what these men sacrificed, then ultimately you're going to wind up forgetting what they sacrificed for, too," Flood said. "It's easy to forget how important that is when you aren't reminded of the cost of it." Flood said his concern about how military history is taught partly comes from his own experience in school, though he says that may or may not be typical. He said he frequently hears from viewers who once thought they disliked history, only to become interested in it when they begin hearing the stories of the people who lived it. To look beyond his own experience, Flood created a survey that drew more than 1,100 responses from 49 states. He focused in particular on 81 eighth graders whose teachers administered the survey in class and whose families did not watch his videos. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The results showed a striking divide between their knowledge of pop culture and military history. Among eighth graders, 98% of those who took the survey knew that Travis Kelce married Taylor Swift — while just 6% could name a Medal of Honor recipient, Flood said. Only one in eight could name an American hero from World War II — while nearly a third selected actor Woody Harrelson when asked to identify a war hero. At the same time, 64% of the students said someone in their own family had served in the military. The students did not appear uninterested in history. Most rated their history class a four or five out of five, and one student offered an idea about how to make the subject more meaningful. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "It should feel less like a memory test and more like we're learning about real people," the student wrote. Flood said that is why he believes storytelling can make history resonate in a way that memorizing dates and locations may not. "You can still teach the big picture of World War II, but you can teach it through the lens of an individual," he said. "And not only is it more entertaining, it's more compelling, but it also makes it easier for kids and people in general to relate to." He said viewers repeatedly asked for versions of his stories that they could share with their children. One story very much on Flood's mind is that of Vietnam War Medal of Honor recipient Roy Benavidez — who recovered from a severe injury, returned to military service and later helped save fellow service members during a lengthy firefight. Flood said he has drawn on lessons from Benavidez's story while dealing with injuries in his own life. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "If Roy Benavidez could live through what he did, I mean, I can get through this," Flood recalled thinking. "I think hearing these lessons, especially at a young age to kids, is very powerful." The response to Flood's online work ultimately helped inspire "Heroes Erased," his children's book series focused on 10 American heroes from World War II. He said viewers had repeatedly asked for versions of his stories that they could share with their children. Flood said he hopes the book project encourages others to keep telling the stories of the people behind American military history. "Everybody wants to hear these stories," he said. "Everybody wants to be excited about history." Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links. For Flood, the message extends beyond Veterans Day. "I don't think that you should just go out and learn these stories because you're supposed to honor veterans," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I think there's actual value to be learned from hearing these stories and taking them in."

articles.title: Amazon’s Ring debuts security robots including a drone
articles.summary: Amazon’s Ring has launched an indoor security drone, the company said Tuesday, offering homeowners room-to-room surveillance where a fixed camera cannot reach.
articles.body: Amazon’s Ring has launched an indoor security drone, the company said Tuesday, offering homeowners room-to-room surveillance where a fixed camera cannot reach. The $250 Ring Drone Camera offers exactly what the product’s name implies — the technology to capture moving images from a lens affixed to a small quadcopter drone, according to the company. Ring founder and chief inventor Jamie Siminoff said his customers have been asking for an expansion of the company’s popular doorbell cameras without having to install more cameras around the house. “For years, customers told us they wanted eyes in the places a fixed camera couldn’t reach, and peace of mind in the spots they’d never want one,” Siminoff said in a statement released by the company Tuesday. “The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be. That kind of invention is hard, and it takes time. But we kept at it until we got it right—and that’s Ring Robotics. It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have.” The drone provides “wall-to-wall coverage,” according to Ring, with 148-degree peripheral vision and the ability to rotate 360 degrees to quickly spot potential threats. LED lights also equip it to work in “low-light environments” so that homeowners can “always get clear, crisp video,” the company said. Ring also rolled out its $1,000 Ring Rover Cam, tailored for businesses. The tool could be used to “investigate a disturbance” or be set to do “regular sweeps” of the property. “Get a closer look wherever and whenever you need it without the cost and complexity of wiring up every corner of every room,” the company said. Both pieces of equipment require a subscription fee of $5 per month or $60 annually, a customer service rep told NBC News.

articles.title: Huntingdon train attack driver had '10 seconds' to change line
articles.summary: Andrew Johnson tells jurors he heard over the intercom "'there's a knifeman stabbing people'".
articles.body:
The driver of a high-speed train where a mass stabbing took place said he had "probably about 10 seconds" to decide to switch to the slow line before making an unscheduled stop.

Andrew Johnson was driving the London-bound LNER service on 1 November last year when the train stopped at Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire.

Giving evidence, Johnson told jurors at Cambridge Crown Court he heard someone on the intercom "screaming 'there's a knifeman stabbing people'".

Anthony Williams, 33, of Peterborough, denies 10 counts of attempted murder on the train.

He is also charged with four other attempted murders following earlier incidents in Peterborough and London.

Johnson told jurors the train was running "bang on time" as it travelled at about 122mph (196km/h) in the Abbots Ripton area of Cambridgeshire.

He said there was an unusual alarm "which indicated someone was trying to open one of the passenger doors".

"I have five seconds to override or the train will stop immediately," he explained.

He said if the train stopped it would take about a mile or 30 seconds to come to a standstill.

Johnson said he picked up the intercom to that door but received no response and thought "Saturday night, someone's messing around".

He said while he was speaking to the train manager to ask her to investigate "someone over-spoke us" and he heard someone "screaming 'there's a knifeman stabbing people'".

He thought the "best thing to do was to get to a platform" and the voice of the individual "really drove that home".

Johnson said he had "probably about 10 seconds" to switch to the slow line, adding: "I just knew that was the right option, it just came instinctively."

He pressed the urgent button and told a signaller "get me to Huntingdon and get me the police".

Jurors heard Johnson "could hear banging and screaming" on the cab door, and he said: "It was incredibly loud, and people were begging for me to open the door as well."

Johnson explained that he had to remain in his seat, adding: "My mind was completely focused on one thing and that was to get the train to Huntingdon."

When the train pulled into Huntingdon at 19:44 GMT, the court heard he had to override the system to open the doors because it was "not a programmed stop for us", taking about 15 seconds.

He said he saw passengers on the platform and "they didn't just run, they sprinted like I'd never seen before".

The court heard that throughout the incident, Johnson never had sight of Williams.

As well as arguing Williams was attempting to murder the 10 people on the train, prosecutors allege that on 31 October he tried to kill three people in Peterborough.

He is also charged with attempting to murder a teenager in the early hours of 1 November on a DLR train in east London.

Whether Williams carried out the attacks is not in question - the court has been told - but jurors must consider whether he intended to kill.

articles.title: Inside devastated front-line city of Slovyansk that Russia wants Ukraine to give up
articles.summary: The BBC gains rare access to a specialist drone unit defending the eastern city of Slovyansk from heavy Russian fire.
articles.body:
The dangers in Slovyansk are clear from the start.

"If I say run, you run," Tetiana tells us. She and her colleague Yasha are escorting us into a city now under constant bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.

It is raining and cloudy as we enter the city, and our military escorts call this "good" weather, meaning it is bad for drones.

But the threat is still there, and Yasha keeps his eyes peeled on the skies, while 21-year-old Tetiana scours her phone for the latest military intelligence on likely threats from the air.

They are members of a drone unit who call themselves Peaky Blinders and their distinctive emblem is a flat cap of the type made popular by the cult BBC TV series, although theirs are camouflaged.

Slovyansk is one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control.

Russia wants Kyiv to give up the fortress cities and they are central to talks on a possible peace deal that have resumed after nine months between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.

Ukrainians worry that doing so would make it much easier for Russia to advance further west, including to the capital Kyiv.

Once inside the city, we leave our vehicles hidden under the cover of trees and venture out on foot. Yasha carries a shotgun – a last resort to shoot down Russian drones. In halting English, Tetiana tells us walking is safer than travelling by car.

Abandoned vehicles litter the streets – recently destroyed by remotely operated Russian first-person view drones. The anti-drone netting that covers the roads is no guarantee of safety.

Tetiana shows us a video on her phone taken a few days earlier.

You can hear several drones buzzing above her, and then the cacophony of small arms fire as Ukrainian forces try to shoot them down. Tetiana admits it can be scary but explains how she felt compelled to help her country, abandoning her dreams of becoming an opera singer.

Slovyansk is now a husk of its former self. Very few buildings have been left unscathed, with many reduced to rubble.

Tetiana shows us a school recently destroyed by Russian glide bombs. Across the road there is a gaping hole in an abandoned residential block. Broken glass litters the pavement. The few shops still functioning are boarded up – making it hard to distinguish what is still open. Most have closed.

Tetiana says the Russians are doing everything they can to intimidate people and drive them out of the city. That, she says, "is their strategy – to make people leave in chaos, gathering up their last belongings and fleeing amid enormous fear and suffering. They want people to have nowhere left to live".

It is a familiar pattern already seen in other Ukrainian towns and cities in the Donbas – like Pokrovsk and Bakhmut. These are now ghost towns reduced to rubble, but eventually falling into Russian hands.

Russia has already taken nearly 90% of the Donbas – made up of the regions of Luhansk and Donetsk - but its advances this year have all but stalled in the face of strong Ukrainian resistance.

The White House is sounding positive about the revived talks in Abu Dhabi, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's refusal to cede the territory.

October was the deadliest month for Russian troops since the start of its full-scale invasion – with more than 54,000 killed or injured, according to Ukraine's general staff. Despite this, Russian forces are still making life in the Fortress Belt cities almost impossible.

Before the war, Slovyansk was a city of more than 200,000 people. Less than 10% of those remain and the population diminishes by the day.

But amid the wail of near constant air raid warnings, there are still signs of people clinging on to life here. Iryna works in one of the city's last remaining coffee shops. Slovyansk is where she was born.

"I'm forced to walk around crying," she tells me. "How can they do this?"

Life, she says, has become incredibly difficult. She has already lost her house. But despite her tears, there is still defiance: "I won't leave Slovyansk. This is my home."

Inga, 53, was also born and raised here and continues to work in the city despite the danger.

"It's stressful. Honestly, I don't even know what to say," she says, but she is staying because of what she calls the "fear of the unknown".

"I simply have nowhere to go, and I don't have the money to leave or support myself afterwards." Nor, she says, is there anywhere else in Ukraine she would consider truly safe.

We first met the Omega National Guard Special Forces drone unit two years ago fighting in the Kharkiv region, in north-eastern Ukraine.

Just four of the original team remain - the rest have moved to other units, or they have been wounded or killed.

Among the dead was the brother of the man in charge of the unit, Oleksandr, who now describes his unit as his family.

He jokes it is just like the Peaky Blinders TV show – "but without the crime and the drugs". Back at their base they share a meal every evening.

Oleksandr reads out a prayer of thanks for surviving another day – he says it strengthens their spirits. The meal is accompanied by classical music played on a speaker. It helps drown out the noise of the explosions nearby.

"I feel this is the most difficult situation we've ever faced," says Oleksandr, who underlines the importance of holding the line.

"We must be here to inflict maximum damage on the enemy. We're fighting here because this is where the most intense phase of the war is taking place. Russia's claim that they will reach the borders of the Donbas, seize it, and then the war will end is absolutely false," he insists.

The remaining fortress belt cities provide Ukraine with a strong defensive line and are a major obstacle to any Russian advance. The saturation of drones in the area is also now making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance here.

Peace talks may have resumed, but Oleksandr notes they have not led to anything so far.

"I really want this war to end," he says, "but do I believe these negotiations will succeed? No, I don't really believe they will".

The next morning we are not the only ones making an exit. A dozen civilians have arrived at an evacuation point in the centre to be escorted out.

They hold all the belongings they can carry and are taken into a bunker for their safety. Outside there is another heavy blast of small arms fire, signalling more drones are nearby.

Alina Shyrko, herself a resident of Slovyansk, is co-ordinating the move of civilians out of the city and says the situation has deteriorated rapidly over the past few months. Families with children have already been ordered to leave.

"Everyone is thinking about leaving," she says, "I'm thinking about it too."

Ukraine still holds Slovyansk but its lifeblood, its people, are ebbing away.

articles.title: Amazon to refund $3 million to Prime customers over six-step cancellation process; also agrees to donate $1 million to charities and allocate $1.5 million to consumer protection
articles.summary: Amazon has agreed to pay $3 million to eligible customers in Arizona following allegations that it made cancelling its Prime memberships unnecessarily
articles.body: Amazon has agreed to pay $3 million to eligible customers in Arizona following allegations that it made cancelling its Prime memberships unnecessarily difficult. The settlement comes after Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes accused the retail giant of using a complicated cancellation system that allegedly prevented customers from easily ending subscriptions they no longer wanted.According to a report by the Arizona Daily Star, the agreement requires Amazon to provide $3 million to the Attorney General's Office for distribution among eligible consumers. The company will also pay $1.5 million towards a fund used to investigate consumer fraud and educate residents about protecting themselves, along with another $1.5 million to cover the state's legal expenses.Additionally, Amazon has agreed to donate $1 million to charitable organisations selected by Mayes, all of which work towards providing food to people in need.Amazon Prime customers allegedly faced six steps to cancel membershipsThe lawsuit, filed by Mayes in 2024 under Arizona's consumer fraud laws, focused on Amazon's online Prime membership cancellation process. The state alleged that customers had to navigate at least six separate steps to end their subscriptions, despite the company's advertisements claiming that members could cancel anytime.According to the Attorney General's legal filings, customers were required to:Log in to Prime Central.Click on 'Manage membership'.Select 'End membership'.Click on 'Continue to cancel'.Again select 'Continue to cancel'.Finally, click on 'End now'.Mayes argued that the process created unnecessary hurdles for customers attempting to leave the subscription service. The state alleged that the system was designed to discourage cancellations and retain members who might otherwise have ended their subscriptions.Amazon allegedly reduced cancellations by 14%In her legal filings, Mayes claimed that the cancellation system had helped Amazon reduce membership cancellations by 14% at one point, as fewer customers managed to reach the final cancellation page.The state also argued that customers were not informed about these hurdles when signing up for the service.Amazon Prime costs $139 annually in the US and offers benefits such as free delivery, sometimes on the same day, along with other membership services.Mayes also highlighted the financial significance of the subscription programme, claiming that Prime members spend an average of $1,400 annually on Amazon purchases, more than twice the amount spent by non-Prime customers.Her filings further cited approximately $25 billion in annual Prime subscription revenue, with around three-quarters of that amount coming from US subscribers.Amazon denies wrongdoing despite agreeing to settlementThe Arizona agreement follows a separate settlement between Amazon and the Federal Trade Commission last year, which required the company to change its cancellation practices.That deal included a $1 billion civil penalty and $1.5 billion in customer refunds. However, Mayes continued with her own lawsuit, arguing that the federal settlement might not cover everyone who experienced difficulties cancelling Prime memberships or compensate them for all their costs.Richie Taylor, spokesperson for the Arizona Attorney General's Office, said the state's objective was to recover as much money as possible for consumers affected by the alleged practices.In a statement, Mayes said, "Arizonans should be able to cancel a subscription as easily as they signed up for it, without jumping through endless hoops."She added that the settlement would provide restitution to eligible residents and that her office would continue standing up for consumers dealing with unwanted subscriptions.However, Amazon has denied engaging in any activity that violates Arizona law. Under the consent judgment, the company does not admit wrongdoing, and attorneys representing the state have agreed not to claim that its past, present or future business practices are illegal.Amazon faces another Arizona lawsuit over product listings and Buy BoxWhile the Prime cancellation dispute has reached a settlement, Amazon continues to fight another lawsuit filed by Mayes in 2024. The separate case, pending before Maricopa County Superior Court, concerns how products and sellers are displayed on Amazon's website.The Attorney General alleges that the company's product listings are designed to make shoppers believe that the first offer displayed is the best available deal, even when other sellers may be offering the same product at a lower price.The lawsuit specifically challenges Amazon's Buy Box feature, which allows customers to add a selected seller's product to their shopping cart with a single click.Mayes claims that the algorithm behind the feature favours products sold directly by Amazon or third-party sellers participating in its Fulfillment by Amazon programme. The programme charges retailers fees for services including inventory storage, packaging, shipping, returns and customer communication.According to the lawsuit, sellers who do not participate in the programme may receive less prominent placement, even when they offer identical products at lower prices. The state alleges that this could lead customers to pay more than necessary.The lawsuit further claims that nearly 98% of purchases are made through the Buy Box because shoppers may assume that the prominently displayed offer represents the best available price.Amazon has denied the accusations, arguing that the lawsuit was filed without reviewing a single company document and reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of how its business operates.No hearing date has been set in the separate case, which Amazon continues to contest.You use AI every day. articles.title: Photos: Crowds greet Pope Leo in Argentina after 40-year wait
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV urges Argentinians to emulate their saints during his landmark visit, drawing crowds not seen for decades.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV has urged Argentinians to follow the “holy example” of the country’s saints and build a more “fraternal and caring nation”, as an estimated 650,000 people packed the central city of Cordoba for Mass.

The 71-year-old pontiff, on a 12‑day Latin America tour less than a month after lung cancer surgery, on Tuesday celebrated the liturgy on the esplanade of a military aircraft factory.

The Vatican said it was attended by 650,000 pilgrims, following Monday’s Mass in Buenos Aires, where about 2.5 million worshippers gathered – the largest of his pontificate so far.

In Cordoba, Leo listed Argentinian saints and blessed figures as examples of a unity “between passion for the Gospel and commitment to building a fraternal and caring nation”, urging citizens to evangelise “at school and in the square, in the family and with friends, in the countryside and in the city, at the dairy farm and in the office”.

Faithful travelled from across the country after nearly 40 years without a papal visit. “It was quite a journey,” said Erika Vinales, who travelled 2,000km (1,242 miles) from Patagonia with fellow teacher Elena Llanquenao.

Throughout his three days in Argentina, Leo has repeatedly challenged President Javier Milei’s right-wing government to make the economy more inclusive, protect trade unions and reverse funding cuts that hurt the poor and people with disabilities.

After nearly 40 years without a papal visit, faithful from the far north to Patagonia drove for hours and days to see the pontiff. [Nicolas Aguilera/AP Photo]
Leo recalled Cordoba as a “land of saints”, home to some of Argentina’s most famous missionaries. [Andrew Medichini/AP Photo]
“We are all called to holiness,” Leo said. “Today, it is our turn to follow the radiant example of holiness they have left with us.” [Gustavo Garello/AP Photo]
Leo spoke of Argentina’s history of “reasons for gratitude and painful memories”, urging each generation to confront past injustices. [Gustavo Garello/AP Photo]
The gathering reflected the broad appeal Leo has enjoyed in Argentina, extending beyond regular churchgoers. [Andrew Medichini/AP Photo]

articles.title: Robert Fox left his house to run an errand and never returned. Seven months later, his wife of 25 years is still searching for answers
articles.summary: Robert Fox disappeared on March 19, 2026, in South Point, Ohio. He was out running an errand, but never returned home. The Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office is investigating.
articles.body: In a town of fewer than 4,000 people, it’s not unusual to find love close to home. Letitia Fox met her future husband, Robert, when they were young. He was her best friend’s brother. “His sister’s still my best friend,” Letitia told Dateline. Years of friendship eventually turned into marriage. Robert and Letitia Fox have been married for 25 years. They live in South Point, Ohio, down the street from the house Letitia grew up in. It’s a close-knit community that has shaped their lives for decades. That community keeps her going today. “I’ve had people walk up to me and just hug me, people I don’t even know,” she said. Even those who know her well wonder how she’s holding it together. Because in March, her husband, 47-year-old Robert Fox disappeared. “I keep going and fighting because I have to find him, and I’m going to find him,” Letitia said. March 19, 2026, was a day like any other at the Foxes’ home. “We’d get up for work every day and he would take me to work,” Letitia said. The couple carpooled because Letitia’s shift started before Robert’s and ended later than his. Letitia says that after they got home from work that night, Robert told her he had to run an errand. He asked her to come along, but she stayed at home. “He gave me a kiss and told me he loved me,” she explained. Robert was dropping off traffic cones at the home of an acquaintance, Lynn Pauley, whose daughter was learning to drive. Robert had offered to lend them cones to use for practice. Letitia says she expected Robert to be back within a half hour, maybe a bit longer if he got caught up chatting. Lynn’s house was a 10-minute drive from theirs. Just before 8 p.m., Letitia got a call from Robert that he was waiting for Lynn, but would be home shortly. When he still hadn’t arrived by 8:30 p.m., she called him, but he didn’t answer. That’s when she knew something was wrong. “His daughter’s calling him. We’re all sitting there like, ‘This isn’t like him not to call or answer the phone back,’” she said. Letitia waited anxiously at home for a phone call, her mind racing through possibilities. Around 10 p.m., she drove by Lynn’s house and saw that the traffic cones were there, so she figured Robert had at least made it to Lynn’s. At midnight, after her son got off work, the family began searching for Robert. Letitia drove around South Point with her son, daughter, and her daughter’s best friend, looking for Robert. After a couple hours of searching, Letitia thought of checking out apartment buildings. “The first one we pull into, we go around, come back, there’s my Jeep parked back in at the Lawrence Village Apartments,” she said. The car was unlocked, but Robert was nowhere to be found. His phone and keys were also missing. The Foxes knew a handful of people who lived in the apartment complex, but Letitia says they weren’t close enough to anyone there for Robert to be visiting at that hour. She started calling out to anyone who was awake to help her locate her husband. “The woman in the front says she could see the Jeep going by,” Letitia said. The woman had security camera footage, which Letitia watched. She says she recognized the person in the video as Lynn Pauley. “You see Lynn get out the car, back it in. He’s trying to lock the door, but he’s unlocking the door. And he takes off walking with stuff in his hand.” Letitia shared the video with Dateline. In the footage, a man wearing overalls is seen exiting the Jeep at 10:24 p.m. No one else is visible. Dateline reached out to Lynn Pauley but has not received a response. Letitia and the children eventually returned home to try to catch some sleep. She says within minutes of getting home, she got a call from Robert’s employer who said Robert hadn’t shown up for work. Letitia says the employer had tried calling Robert before reaching out to her. “They’re like, ‘But some man answered his phone,’” Letitia said. “So I call it, and the apartment manager answers the phone.” According to Letitia, it was the manager of Lawrence Village Apartments, who told her that Robert’s phone had been found in a drain on the property. Letitia says she and her daughter went to retrieve the phone and check out where it was found. Robert kept his ID and cards in the back of his phone. “It was all there. Nothing had been used and touched,” she said. According to Letitia, her sister-in-law found Robert’s car keys later that day on the grounds of the apartment complex. Around 8 a.m., Letitia and her daughter went to Lynn’s house, just across the interstate from the Lawrence Village Apartments. Letitia says you can walk there in a couple of minutes. She says she and her daughter confronted Lynn with Robert’s phone, and showed him the security video of him parking Robert’s car. Letitia says she did not get any useful information from Lynn, so she went back to the apartment parking lot and called the police to report her husband missing. The Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office took the report. Letitia says she gave the officers Robert’s phone and car keys, and shared the security video of the parking lot. Lawrence County Sheriff’s Detective Sergeant Brad Layman, who is handling the case, confirmed to Dateline that Lynn Pauley is the man seen parking Robert’s Jeep in the security video. Layman says the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office met with Pauley on March 20 and “got a statement from him.” Investigators spoke with numerous residents of Lawrence Village Apartments and community members and collected additional security footage from the area. “There was probably about 15 search warrants done in those first three or four days, including Mr. Pauley’s property, where we had cadaver dogs, drones, ATVs,” Layman told Dateline. He says the Sheriff’s Office searched neighboring properties numerous times as well. Layman says Robert’s phone was sent to a forensic crime lab for analysis, and investigators are awaiting the results. They hope his text messages will help investigators determine what happened to Robert the night he disappeared. Layman confirmed that Lynn Pauley is a person of interest in Robert’s disappearance, but emphasized that investigators are looking at others as well. “We have numerous persons of interest that we’re looking at and looking into,” he said. No suspects have been named in the case. Layman stresses that information from the public is critical to the investigation. “The more people we can get talking about it, the better off we’re gonna be.” The Fox family won’t stop talking about it. It’s now been more than seven months since Robert kissed his wife goodbye to leave for a quick errand and never returned. In July, Letitia marked their 25th wedding anniversary without Robert. “He was our everything. He made sure our family ran, and now it’s me,” Letitia said. “I know my family needs me, and Robert is counting on me to find him.” Robert is 5’5”, 230 lbs. He has blue eyes and brown hair. He was last seen wearing a blue King’s Daughters T-shirt, khaki pants, and white sneakers. Anyone with information regarding Robert’s disappearance is encouraged to contact the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office at 740-532-3525 and dial extension 8 for Investigations. If you have a story to share with Dateline, please submit it here.

articles.title: Myanmar summons German envoy over controversial video
articles.summary: Mathias Licharz calls for the ‘unconditional’ release of ousted politicians, including former leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
articles.body:
Myanmar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has summoned the head of mission at the German embassy in the country over a Facebook video calling for authorities to “unconditionally release” ousted politicians such as former leader Aung San Suu Kyi .

The ministry said in a statement on Tuesday that Mathias Licharz in the video “appeared to fuel opposition to the host country and its Government, thereby inciting internal unrest”.

Licharz met Deputy Foreign Minister Ko Ko Kyaw, was “warned against the video” and handed an aide-memoire, the ministry said.

“The Deputy Minister strongly warned against recurrence of such act and informed him that any similar conduct would be treated with utmost seriousness and would take appropriate actions,” the ministry said.

Licharz posted the video on Sunday, standing outside the former Yangon residence of Win Myint, the figurehead president of Aung San Suu Kyi ‘s government that was removed in a 2021 coup.

The German diplomat said in his message, marking Win Myint’s 75th birthday, that the United Nations still regards him as the “legitimate president” of Myanmar.

In the video, he called for authorities to “unconditionally release all those who are arbitrarily detained, including Win Myint and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi” – using the affectionate term by which Aung San Suu Kyi ‘s supporters refer to her.

Germany’s embassy in Myanmar did not immediately comment.

Win Myint was jailed in the February 2021 military coup, ending Myanmar’s decade-long democratic experiment.

Since then, pro-democracy rebels rose up and long-simmering ethnic minority rebellions challenging central rule boiled over .

Authorities said in April he had been pardoned of his post-coup convictions – charges that supporters and analysts say were confected to oust the government.

However, Licharz said in his video message his efforts to meet Win Myint had been unfruitful.

“There is only one conclusion,” he said. “U Wint Myint is not a free man. He’s not allowed to meet with whom he would like to meet, and he’s not allowed to communicate independently,” he added, using a male honorific.

The military leadership behind the coup organised elections, installing a nominally civilian government this year, although analysts regard it as a fig leaf for ongoing military rule.

“Should the Charge d’Affaires choose to recognize U Win Myint as President and wish to discontinue his service in Myanmar, the Ministry would have no objection,” the Foreign Ministry statement said on Tuesday.

Aung San Suu Kyi remains detained but was moved to house arrest in the capital Naypyidaw this year, authorities say, where access to the 81-year-old Nobel Peace Prize laureate remains tightly controlled.

articles.title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Lindsay Clancy judge denies double jeopardy motion and explains jury notes after deadlock
articles.summary: Judge William Sullivan denied Lindsay Clancy's double jeopardy motion, ruling there was manifest necessity for the mistrial in her murder case.
articles.body: The Massachusetts judge overseeing the murder case against Lindsay Clancy has denied her motion to dismiss the case on double jeopardy claims, clearing the way for a retrial in the strangling deaths of her three young children that some experts believe could have a better chance at a guilty verdict. "Because the Court concludes that there was a manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury’s deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy’s right not to be placed in double jeopardy," Judge William Sullivan wrote in a 17-page order and memorandum made public Monday. Clancy's 26-day trial ended with a deadlocked jury on Sept. 4, with jurors later saying publicly that 11 of them accepted her insanity defense and one wanted to find her guilty of first-degree murder for what the holdout called the "methodical" slayings of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months. LINDSAY CLANCY DEFENSE FILES MOTION TO DISMISS UNDER DOUBLE JEOPARDY GROUNDS, WITH FOCUS ON HOLDOUT JUROR Had the motion been granted, Clancy would not face a potential second trial, said Randolph Rice, a trial attorney and former prosecutor who is not connected to the case. Now, he says, the order gives prosecutors a chance to address what went wrong with their case in the first trial. "I think there's real possibility that DA [Tim] Cruz says, 'We're going back to trial ... and we have learned from our mistakes,'" Rice said. Among the lessons learned, Rice said, may be that Plymouth County prosecutors did not show jurors enough empathy when presenting their case after 11 of the 12 jurors voted against them. What a second trial may look like remains unclear as prosecutors have so far declined to publicly commit to bringing the same or different charges. Deliberations began on Aug. 27. On Sept. 1, they sent the first of several notes explaining their deadlocked situation. "After many hours of deliberation, we are unable to come to a unanimous verdict," that first note said, according to Sullivan, who instructed them to keep trying. They sent a similar note on Sept. 2, and Sullivan, without objection from lawyers on either side, read them what's known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge — an instruction given to hung jurors encouraging them to reexamine their views with an open mind while reminding jurors they should not abandon honestly held beliefs to reach their verdict. On Sept. 3, Sullivan received another note reading, "A member of the jury is unable to follow the instructions regarding reasonable doubt. How should we proceed?" ATTORNEY FOR LONE HOLDOUT JUROR IN LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL PUSHES BACK ON CLAIMS OF REFUSING THE LAW In his order, Sullivan wrote that he was skeptical of the allegation that the holdout was "genuinely" unable to follow instructions regarding reasonable doubt and decided to hold a "limited inquiry" into each juror's ability to follow the law. Prosecutors had opposed voir dire, and the defense asked for the holdout to be replaced with an alternate. The defense then asked for the judge to ask the foreperson to expand on what she meant in her latest note, and prosecutors objected, arguing that a question like that would improperly intrude into the deliberation process. Sullivan agreed with the commonwealth and asked each juror, "Are you able to follow my instructions on the law that were given to you earlier in the trial?" LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR WON'T HAVE TO TURN OVER PHONE OR FACE INQUIRY, JUDGE SAYS Each juror answered "affirmatively and credibly," Sullivan wrote. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Prosecutors and the defense agreed that the court should also reinstruct the jury, as a whole, about reasonable doubt, and Sullivan did so. Afterward, however, Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, again asked for the holdout to be replaced with an alternate, and Sullivan denied his motion. LINDSAY CLANCY'S PUSH TO PROBE HOLDOUT JUROR HITS SNAG BEFORE PIVOTAL RETRIAL HEARING Later on Sept. 3, the foreperson sent another note, directly accusing the holdout of ignoring reasonable doubts about the case, according to Sullivan. "This is why we cannot come to a unanimous decision." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB Jurors were sent home for the day. Before deliberations resumed on Sept. 4, Sullivan and counsel on both sides discussed the latest note. Sullivan gave jurors another instruction on reasonable doubt and following the law and told them that future notes should not identify anyone's vote based on their juror number. Two hours later, with no movement in the deliberation room, Sullivan said he planned to declare a mistrial, over Reddington's objection. SEND US A TIP He granted a one-hour stay as the defense appealed to the state's Supreme Judicial Court. A single justice summarily denied the defense’s emergency request, then Sullivan declared a mistrial. LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER SAYS HE PLANS NEW MOTION TO DISMISS AFTER JURORS SPEAK OUT ON MISTRIAL: REPORT Clancy's defense later filed a motion to dismiss on double jeopardy grounds, arguing that there was no "manifest necessity" for the court to declare a mistrial and that as a result, a new trial would violate Clancy's Fifth Amendment rights. articles.title: US Army soldier arrested in UK on suspicion of espionage related to Russia
articles.summary: A 41-year-old United States Army soldier was arrested in the United Kingdom on Tuesday on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, according to London’s Metropolitan Police.
articles.body: A 41-year-old United States Army soldier was arrested in the United Kingdom on Tuesday on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, according to London’s Metropolitan Police. The unnamed soldier was arrested by British counterterror police “working closely with US authorities, US Military and the FBI,” the Metropolitan Police said in a statement. He remains in custody at a London police station. “The 41-year-old man was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday, 10 November,” the release said. “He was arrested on suspicion of offenses under Section 1 and Section 3 of the National Security Act 2023.” Section 1 of the act concerns handling “protected information,” and Section 3 concerns “assisting a foreign intelligence service.” “As part of the investigation officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire,” police said. “The country to which the allegations relate is Russia.” Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command, said in the release that the “senior soldier” in question was “entrusted with sensitive information.” FBI Director Kash Patel was quoted in the release stating that the arrest “involves allegations of espionage.” “While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners,” Patel said. CNN has reached out to Russia’s embassies in Washington and London for comment. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.body: A man accused of being part of a plot to kidnap and murder Indian-origin Sikh man Avtar Singh in California has been arrested in Mexico, months after the shocking abduction from a gurdwara in Tracy.Alberto Alonso Alencastro, 25, was apprehended in Mexico in coordination with Mexican law enforcement authorities and then brought back to San Joaquin County, where he was booked into jail, the San Joaquin County Sheriff's Office announced on November 7.Alencastro is one of three men accused of kidnapping and killing Singh, 57, who was abducted from the Gurdwara Gur Nanak Parkash in Tracy on February 17. The other two suspects, Alfonso Cresencio Segura Arellano, 20, and Barnabe Antonio Segura Arellano, 22, remain at large.Singh's body was discovered near Lake Berryessa on February 20, three days after his abduction. Surveillance footage showed three men forcing him into a white crossover-style SUV in broad daylight.The killing shocked the local Sikh community, particularly because Singh's three young children, who were triplets, were left alone inside the temple when he was taken. Singh lived on the gurdwara premises with his wife and children and was a longtime volunteer who served as the temple's head cook.Mistaken identity behind kidnappingInvestigators believe Singh was not the intended target and was abducted in a case of mistaken identity.According to the sheriff's office, the actual target was a person living in Canada who had allegedly been receiving threats linked to a stolen cargo trailer. Investigators travelled to Canada between February 25 and 27 and established a connection between the threats and the trailer theft.Authorities said the suspects allegedly wanted to pursue and kill the person they believed had stolen the cargo. But Singh was apparently mistaken for that individual.In September, authorities identified the three men from Vallejo as suspects and announced that they had been indicted on charges including murder with special circumstances and kidnapping. Investigators also seized a white SUV believed to have been used in the abduction.The San Joaquin County Sheriff's Office thanked the FBI and Mexican federal law enforcement authorities for helping apprehend Alencastro.The two remaining suspects are still being sought. It carries the green bean casserole, the sweet potatoes, the macaroni and cheese, the stuffing, and whatever your aunt brings that nobody can name. A good one goes from the oven to the table to the fridge without trouble and it heats evenly, so you don’t end up with a scorched edge and a cold middle. If yours is chipped, warped or just too small for the crowd you’re hosting, now is a good time to replace it before the holiday rush. Below, I rounded up some of the best casserole dishes, including classic ceramic and stoneware bakers and more budget-friendly glass sets. The best casserole dishes Every option on this list has a four-star average rating or greater at retailers like Amazon, Walmart and Crate and Barrel. Caraway’s rectangle pan has a ceramic nonstick coating, so cleanup is easy, even with baked-on cheese. It’s oven-safe up to 550 degrees, and the handles make it simple to carry from the oven to the table. When you need a deeper dish, reach for this Pyrex casserole pan. The included lid also makes it easy to transport, so it’s a good choice if you’re bringing a side to someone else’s house. The pans are made from borosilicate glass that’s oven-, freezer-, microwave and dishwasher-safe and come with lids for transport or storing leftovers after the meal. Want more from NBC Selected? articles.title: Republicans elect Trump ally Jim Jordan as new US House minority leader
articles.summary: Ohio Congressman Jim Jordan to succeed Mike Johnson as GOP minority leader, promising unity and a robust opposition.
articles.body:
Washington, DC – One week after losing their majority in midterm elections in the United States, Republicans in the US House of Representatives have chosen Congressman Jim Jordan as their new minority leader.

In a secret ballot vote held on Tuesday, the Ohio lawmaker, who was first elected to the US Congress in 2007, won the support of his fellow party members to succeed Mike Johnson as the chamber’s top Republican.

The high-stakes decision comes as Republicans try to chart a path forward after a bruising midterm defeat in which Democrats flipped at least 40 seats nationwide.

Jordan had been vying with current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise for the role, which will carry a host of responsibilities as Republicans prepare to message against at least two years of Democrat-led investigations into US President Donald Trump’s administration and pick a 2028 presidential nominee.

In a reported letter to his fellow Republicans before Tuesday’s vote, Jordan described himself as a “battle-tested” leader who was ready to take on those challenges.

“I know what it will take to lead our Conference in the minority, to stay unified, and to coordinate and calibrate our response to the Democrats’ tactics”, he wrote. “We need a Leadership team that is active and engaged, forward-thinking and straight-shooting”.

Jordan, a top Trump ally, has been an influential voice in the Republican caucus. He cofounded the conservative House Freedom Caucus, which has frustrated many former and current Republican leaders and thwarted party-backed legislation.

The group’s chairman, Republican Congressman Andy Harris, congratulated Jordan after the vote, calling him “a fierce fighter, uniter, principled conservative, and relentless advocate for the American people”.

“Jim is exactly the right man for the job to fight back against the radical, crazy agenda of Democrats”, Harris said in a statement.

As the current chairman of the House Oversight Committee, Jordan has used his power to look into what he has argued is the weaponisation of government against Trump. He has led the panel’s investigations into former US Special Counsel Jack Smith and Fulton County, Georgia, District Attorney Fani Willis , who both have unsuccessfully prosecuted the president.

Jordan’s allies on the panel were quick to praise his selection.

“Jim is a fighter and a convicted conservative,” Republican Congressman Brandon Gill wrote on social media. “He’s the original congressional brawler and is exactly what our Conference needs to lead us back to the majority”.

Jordan, who once worked as an assistant wrestling coach at Ohio State University, had faced allegations that he had knowledge of sexual abuse of student-athletes by the team’s physician, Dr Richard Strauss, from 1978 to 1998. Jordan has denied the allegations.

He previously made a short-lived bid for US House speaker after Kevin McCarthy was ousted from the role in 2023.

Since then, Jordan has taken a less adversarial approach and aligned himself with Johnson and other members of the current House Republican leadership.

Before Jordan’s victory was sealed, McCarthy went on a podcast after last week’s midterm results to offer some advice to the future leader of the US House Republican conference.

“You can’t just play it day by day”, he told his former aides on Glory, Grief and the Gavel. “You’ve got to have a strategy, because it’ll knock the Democrats off base”.

McCarthy added: “You better have an acknowledgement of what transpired in this last election. Because you got to tell the American people I heard you and it’s going to take time to earn your trust again.”

articles.title: F1 champion Lewis Hamilton visits Gaza border
articles.summary: North Sinai Governor Khaled Megawer briefs the British driver on Egypt-coordinated aid efforts through Rafah crossing.
articles.body:
Seven-time Formula One champion Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s northern El Arish city that borders Gaza to see first-hand efforts to acquire humanitarian aid bound for the Gaza Strip.

North Sinai Governor Khaled Megawer welcomed the British driver on Tuesday and showcased the Egyptian Red Crescent’s aid warehouses.

The governor’s office shared videos on its official Facebook page featuring clips of the visit as Megawer briefed the F1 champion on how relief aid is coordinated.

Hamilton is seen greeting aid workers and inquiring how often they are able to enter Gaza through the Rafah crossing.

Last month , the World Health Organization (WHO) said repeated delays in bringing life-saving medicines, prosthetics and other supplies into Gaza can have “devastating consequences” for Palestinians who urgently need them.

The 41-year-old driver is known to be an advocate for humanitarian and charitable causes.

In 2021, he founded Mission 44, a charity organisation tasked with supporting young people’s access to careers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM).

In 2022, Hamilton was ranked number five on the Sunday Times Giving List, an annual ranking published by the British newspaper, where he was said to have recently donated 20 million British pounds (about $26m) at the time.

The visit comes after heavy rain and harsh floods overwhelmed Gaza this week, killing at least five people, including four children. Floods have displaced thousands in the process and caused sand embankments to collapse on a displacement camp south of Deir el-Balah.

Gaza’s Civil Defence logged more than 2,100 distress calls by Monday and warned that more than 2,000 buildings are at risk of collapsing.

Israeli strikes have subsequently persisted across the enclave, with at least eight people killed in air attacks on Tuesday , including a father and his 13-year-old son in the Gaza Strip, according to local health sources.

Recent cuts to aid and food assistance have caused the situation to continually worsen as people in Gaza grapple for resources.

articles.title: US charges 3 men with plotting terror attacks, including planned assault on UK airbase
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Three men, including one already jailed in the United States, were accused by U. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who p...
articles.body:
NEW YORK (AP) — Three men, including one already jailed in the United States, were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S. as well as a planned assault on a British airbase used by the U.S. Air Force.

Charges against Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court. Only al-Saadi is in custody.

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.

"These defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members," McDonald said. "The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real."

Attorney General Todd Blanche said: "Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government."

The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight on Sept. 27 on suspected explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England.

A sixth suspect, a British-Iranian dual national, was arrested several days later. All the men were released on bail.

British authorities linked the incident to Tehran , and though Iran denied involvement, the arrests prompted the U.S. to withdraw its bombers that had been stationed there. The bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States.

RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.

According to the indictment, al-Saadi used coded language in communications with relatives from jail to direct that money be passed along to others who could carry out attacks.

The indictment alleged that the three men conspired together to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata'ib Hizballah.

In June, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel's war with Iran. He called himself a "prisoner of war." He has been held without bail since. His lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday on the latest development.

Both Kata'ib Hizballah and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have been designated by the U.S. government as foreign terrorist organizations. U.S. prosecutors say Al-Saadi was a Kata'ib Hizballah commander.
